- `src/FileManager.UI/ViewModels/DryRunViewModel.cs:1276`

  ```csharp
  internal static LoadData ComputeLoad(
      IReadOnlyList<DryRunFileRow> rows, string? commonRoot, CancellationToken ct = default)
  // ... the parallel/sequential key-building + index-sort body is repeated verbatim at line 1732 with only
  // the key extractor differing (r.DirPath/r.FileName vs r.HasSource ? SourceDirPath : Primary.DirPath)
  ```


**Why it matters.** This is where the pain actually is. The repo has 128 commits total and DryRunViewModel.cs carries 42 of them — 33% of all commits touch this one file, more than any other file in the repository by a factor of 1.2 over the next (DryRunEngine.cs, 35) and 2.2 over the next UI file (MainWindowViewModel.cs, 19). Fixes are demonstrably being applied twice: commit 507d56c ("Fixed tree view allocations and memory leak") added the identical `Dispose the previous grid source` block twice in a single diff (`git show 507d56c -- src/FileManager.UI/ViewModels/DryRunViewModel.cs | grep -c '^+.*Dispose the previous grid source'` returns 2), and commit 5ff4554 ("Implemented parallelization for more performance") added `Parallel.For` five times in one diff. Every perf fix, every leak fix, and every debounce tweak on this feature is a two-site edit with no compiler check that both sites got it — a leak fix applied to only one tab reproduces on the other. Change-coupling confirms the blast pattern: DryRunViewModel.cs co-changes with DryRunView.axaml in 22 commits and with DryRunViewModelTests.cs in 29.

**Proposed change.** Introduce `internal abstract partial class DryRunTabBase<TRow> : ViewModelBase` in a new file `src/FileManager.UI/ViewModels/DryRun/DryRunTabBase.cs` (same `FileManager.UI.ViewModels` namespace so no XAML `xmlns` or `x:DataType` changes). Move into it, unchanged, every member that the normalized diff shows identical: `_searchDebounce`, `_rebuildGate`, `_applying`, `_all`/`_visible` (typed `List<TRow>`), `_actions`, `PendingRebuild`, `IsRebuilding`, `VisibleRows` (`IReadOnlyList<TRow>`), `Tree`, `TreeSource` + `OnTreeChanged`, `SourceFacets`, `DestinationFacets`, `ShowSourceFacet`, `ShowDestinationFacet`, `SearchText`, `ShowTree`, `ShowAnyFacet`, `ActiveFilterCount`, `FilterLabel`, `CommonRoot`, `CommonRootDisplay`, `StatusFilters`, `AnyStatusSelected`, `SelectedStatusKeys()`, `ClearStatusFilters()`, `OnFacetChanged`, `OnStatusFilterChanged`, `RequestRebuild(bool)`, `RebuildAsync(TimeSpan, CancellationToken)`, and the `RebuildInput`/`RebuildResult` records. Declare exactly six abstract/virtual seam members for the parts the diff shows differing:
  1. `protected abstract IReadOnlyList<TreePillSpec> TreeSpecs { get; }`
  2. `protected abstract IReadOnlyList<DryRunStatusFilter> BuildStatusFilters();` (each tab keeps its own count properties: ProcessedCount vs New/Overwritten)
  3. `protected abstract void CountRow(TRow row, ref TabCounts counts, IDictionary<string,int> sourceCounts, IDictionary<string,int> destinationCounts);` — the body of the ComputeLoad counting loop
  4. `protected abstract string SortKey(TRow row, Dictionary<(string,string?),string> relDirCache);` and `protected abstract string? SortRoot(TRow row);` — the two key/root extractors
  5. `protected abstract bool TryFilterRow(TRow row, in RebuildInput input, out TRow kept);` — the ComputeRebuild per-row predicate; the Sources override returns the row as-is, the Destinations override does the entry-level filter and the `row with { Destinations = kept }` rewrite
  6. `protected abstract IReadOnlyList<DryRunTreeNode> BuildTree(IReadOnlyList<TRow> rows, string? commonRoot, IReadOnlySet<string>? expandedPaths);`
Then reduce `DryRunSourcesTab : DryRunTabBase<DryRunFileRow>` and `DryRunDestinationsTab : DryRunTabBase<DryRunDestinationRow>` to the six overrides plus their own count properties (~90 lines each, from 451/500). Keep both class NAMES, both constructors `(TimeSpan searchDebounce, IDryRunItemActions? actions = null)`, and every public member name and type — DryRunView.axaml binds ~40 paths of the form `{Binding Sources.X}` / `{Binding Destinations.X}` against the concrete types, and those resolve unchanged through a closed generic base. Note ComputeLoad is currently `internal static` and called as `DryRunSourcesTab.ComputeLoad(...)`; make it a protected instance method or keep a per-tab static shim so DryRunViewModel.PrepareReport (line 2474) is unaffected. While the file is open, move the six banner-delimited sections (rows :22, tree :318, facets :1000, tabs :1153, space :2105, shell :2227) into separate files under ViewModels/DryRun/ — no namespace change, so nothing else moves.

**Blast radius.** 4 files, 6 call sites.

Counted, not guessed. `grep -rn 'new DryRunSourcesTab\|new DryRunDestinationsTab' src/ tests/ benchmarks/` yields exactly 6 construction sites: DryRunViewModel.cs:2244 and :2245 (production) plus DryRunViewModelTests.cs:1466, :1511, :1529, :1550. The type names appear only in DryRunViewModel.cs (19 occurrences) and DryRunViewModelTests.cs (4) — grep over src/, tests/ and benchmarks/ finds them nowhere else. Neither type is used as an `x:DataType` in any .axaml (verified against DryRunView.axaml, whose x:DataType keys are DryRunViewModel, DryRunTreeNode, TreePill, DryRunFacetRow, DryRunStatusFilter, DryRunFileRow, DryRunDestinationRow, DryRunDestinationEntry, VolumeSpaceRow, FolderSpaceRow), so neither is on the frozen markup-binding list in the do-not-break register. Files touched: DryRunViewModel.cs, the new DryRunTabBase.cs, DryRunViewModelTests.cs, and benchmarks/FileManager.UI.Benchmarks/ViewModels/DryRunViewModelBenchmarks.cs (only if it names the tabs — it currently reaches them via viewModel.Sources/.Destinations, so likely untouched).

**Verification.** tests/FileManager.UI.Tests/DryRunViewModelTests.cs is 1591 lines / 66 tests and references `Sources.`/`Destinations.` 140 times, covering both tabs' load, facet, status-filter, search-debounce, tree and rebuild paths; it must pass unchanged except for the four `new DryRunSourcesTab(...)` sites, which keep the same constructor signature. Also run DryRunViewModelMemoryTests.cs (which pins the TreeSource-disposal leak that 507d56c fixed in both halves — after the merge it is pinned once and cannot regress on one tab only), DryRunViewSmokeTests.cs (headless XAML load, catches any compiled-binding path that failed to resolve through the generic base), and ResourceKeyContractTests.cs (the TreeSpecs icon/brush key strings must still resolve). Before/after, run benchmarks/FileManager.UI.Benchmarks DryRunViewModelBenchmarks (ApplyReport/PrepareReport/status-filter toggle at 500k files) to confirm the virtual dispatch added to the per-row inner loops of ComputeLoad and ComputeRebuild has not regressed the hot path — if it has, make the seams `static abstract` on a struct type-parameter or pass function pointers instead of virtual calls.

**Verifier note.** Evidence holds and is stronger than most duplication claims: DryRunViewModel.cs:1201-1212 and :1656-1667 are character-identical (including the leak-fix comment), and RebuildAsync (:1484-1540 vs :1970-2026), Clear, SelectedStatusKeys, OnFacetChanged/OnStatusFilterChanged, RequestRebuild, and the RebuildInput/RebuildResult records are byte-identical apart from one log string. Commit 507d56c does add the dispose block twice (verified: grep count 2), and DryRunViewModel.cs does carry 42 of 128 commits. Not critical though — this is maintenance cost, not a live defect, and it is not a frozen-type violation since class names, namespace, constructors and every bound member name are preserved. Downgraded and SCOPED: lift only the state/lifecycle machinery (properties, OnTreeChanged, Load/Clear assignment shape, facet+status plumbing, the rebuild gate and RebuildAsync) and put the seams at whole-operation granularity — `protected abstract LoadData ComputeLoad(...)`, `protected abstract RebuildResult ComputeRebuild(...)`, `protected abstract BuildTree(...)` — one virtual call per load/rebuild, ZERO per-row virtual dispatch. Reject the finding's six per-row abstract seams (CountRow/SortKey/TryFilterRow) outright: they put virtual calls inside loops over up to 500k rows in the repo's hottest UI path, and the finding's own fallback (`static abstract` on a struct type parameter, or function pointers) is a large complexity commitment taken on speculation. Also drop the tacked-on rider about moving the six banner-delimited sections into separate files — that is unrelated file-shuffling bundled into a risky change. Prerequisite: DryRunViewModelMemoryTests + DryRunViewSmokeTests green and the DryRunViewModelBenchmarks ApplyReport/PrepareReport numbers unchanged.

#### `settings-save-after-failed-load-overwrites-real-settings` — A failed settings load leaves the dialog holding constructor defaults, and Save then persists those defaults over the user's real settings.json

| | |
|---|---|
| Lens | error-handling-failure-modes |
| Severity | high (verifier verdict: keep) |
| Confidence | high |
| Effort | trivial |
| Risk flags | changes-behavior, no-test-coverage |

**Claim.** SettingsViewModel.LoadAsync sets an error banner and returns early when GetSettings fails, but leaves every setting at the hard-coded defaults assigned in the constructor. SaveAsync is gated only on IsBusy, so the next Save builds a complete GlobalSettings out of those defaults and persists it — resetting ProfilesDirectory, ScratchDirectory, every thread budget and every drive override.

**Evidence.**

- `src/FileManager.UI/ViewModels/SettingsViewModel.cs:433`

  ```csharp
  if (result.TryGetError(out IpcError? error))
  {
      ErrorMessage = $"Could not load settings: {error.Message}";
      return;
  }
  ```

- `src/FileManager.UI/ViewModels/SettingsViewModel.cs:88`

  ```csharp
  ScratchDirectory.Value = GlobalSettings.DefaultScratchDirectory;
  ProfilesDirectory.Value = GlobalSettings.DefaultProfilesDirectory;
  MaxScanThreads.Value = ScanAutoDefault;
  ```

- `src/FileManager.UI/ViewModels/SettingsViewModel.cs:525`

  ```csharp
  GlobalSettings settings = new()
  {
      ThemeMode = Theme.Value,
      ServiceStartupMode = StartupMode.Value,
      ScratchDirectory = scratch,
      // The profiles directory is changed transactionally via ChangeProfilesDirectory; carry
      // the current value through so a generic Save never resets it to the default.
      ProfilesDirectory = ProfilesDirectory.Value,
  ```

- `src/FileManager.UI/Views/SettingsWindow.axaml:224`

  ```csharp
  <Button Content="Save" Command="{Binding SaveCommand}" Classes="accent" IsEnabled="{Binding !IsBusy}" />
  ```


**Why it matters.** The service can be unreachable for perfectly ordinary reasons — it is a separate process that the UI launches and that can be mid-restart, and IpcGateway drops its client on any transport fault. A user who opens Settings in that window sees a red banner but a fully populated, editable dialog. Changing the theme and clicking Save silently rewrites settings.json: ProfilesDirectory snaps back to %LOCALAPPDATA%\FileManager\profiles, so every profile the user had in a relocated folder disappears from the list (ProfileStore resolves the directory live from settings), and all per-drive thread overrides are deleted. The comment at line 530 shows the author already worried about exactly this class of reset for ProfilesDirectory — the guard just does not cover the failed-load case.

**Proposed change.** In src/FileManager.UI/ViewModels/SettingsViewModel.cs add `private bool _loadFailed;`. Set `_loadFailed = true` on both early-return error paths of LoadAsync (the IPC error branch at line 433 and the catch at line 465) and `_loadFailed = false` immediately after the successful mapping block completes (after line 463). At the top of SaveAsync's try, before building any dictionaries, add:
```
if (_loadFailed)
{
    ErrorMessage = "Settings could not be loaded, so saving would overwrite your stored settings with defaults. Close and reopen this window once the service is reachable.";
    return;
}
```
Do not gate SaveCommand.CanExecute on it — the existing tests in tests/FileManager.UI.Tests/SettingsViewModelTests.cs construct the VM and call SaveCommand without ever calling LoadAsync, and must keep passing (_loadFailed stays false there).

**Blast radius.** 1 file, 2 call sites.

One production file. LoadAsync has 2 failure exits and SaveAsync 1 entry point. 18 existing SaveCommand test invocations across SettingsViewModelTests.cs and SettingsViewModelUndoTests.cs never call LoadAsync, so none change behaviour.

**Verification.** Add a test to tests/FileManager.UI.Tests/SettingsViewModelTests.cs: configure FakeIpcGateway to return an IpcError from GetSettingsAsync, call `await vm.LoadAsync()`, then `await vm.SaveCommand.ExecuteAsync(null)`, and assert `Assert.Empty(gateway.SaveSettingsCalls)` and that ErrorMessage is non-null. Re-run the full FileManager.UI.Tests suite to confirm the 18 existing SaveCommand tests are unaffected.

**Verifier note.** Fully confirmed, and it is the strongest finding in the batch. LoadAsync returns early at SettingsViewModel.cs:433-437 (and :465-470) leaving the constructor defaults from :88-92 intact; SaveAsync (:479) is gated only on IsBusy and unconditionally builds a complete GlobalSettings at :525-541 from those defaults; the Save button is enabled on !IsBusy (SettingsWindow.axaml:224). I also confirmed the dialog opens regardless of load outcome — MainWindowViewModel.OpenSettings awaits LoadAsync then shows the window without checking for an error. So a load failure followed by any Save persists ProfilesDirectory = GlobalSettings.DefaultProfilesDirectory, and since ProfileStore resolves the directory live from settings on every read (ProfileStore.cs:25), a user with a relocated profiles folder loses their whole profile list. The irony is that the comment at :530-531 shows the author already guarded the ProfilesDirectory-reset case for a different path. Fix is one bool and one guard in one file, with the proposed test. Ship it.

#### `disposition-and-audit-failures-reported-as-clean-success` — A post-commit disposition failure — and a failed deletion-audit write — end the job as a clean Succeeded with no error anywhere on the wire

| | |
|---|---|
| Lens | error-handling-failure-modes |
| Severity | high (verifier verdict: keep) |
| Confidence | high |
| Effort | small |
| Risk flags | changes-behavior, no-test-coverage |

**Claim.** JobExecutor records a disposition error only into the on-disk job-closed journal record and the per-job log, then returns `Completed(plan, JobOutcome.Succeeded, null, null, start)` with a null Error. JobOrchestrator therefore publishes JobCompletedEvent and clears _lastError. Separately, SourceDispositionService.Record logs an audit-append failure and returns the record as a success, so a permanently deleted source with no audit row also reports Succeeded.

**Evidence.**

- `src/FileManager.Core/Jobs/JobExecutor.cs:225`

  ```csharp
  string? dispositionError = ApplyDisposition(execution);
  states.Transition(JobState.Closed);
  TryAppend(Close(plan, JobOutcome.Succeeded, skipReason: null, dispositionError));
  ```

- `src/FileManager.Core/Jobs/JobExecutor.cs:237`

  ```csharp
  return Completed(plan, JobOutcome.Succeeded, null, null, start);
  ```

- `src/FileManager.Core/Jobs/JobOrchestrator.cs:229`

  ```csharp
  if (!_pipelineFaulted)
      _lastError = null;
  eventBus.Publish(new JobCompletedEvent { AtUtc = now, Job = dto });
  ```

- `src/FileManager.Core/Disposition/SourceDispositionService.cs:123`

  ```csharp
  Result appended = audit.Append(record);
  if (appended.TryGetError(out string? auditError))
      logger.LogError("Audit append failed for {Path}: {Error}", sourcePath, auditError);   // audit failure never blocks disposition
  ```

- `src/FileManager.Core/Journal/JournalRecord.cs:111`

  ```csharp
  public string? DispositionError { get; init; }     // Phase-6 failure: logged, never rolled back
  ```


**Why it matters.** OnSuccess disposition is the visible half of the product's promise: the user configures "move the source to the Recycle Bin / archive / delete it" and the confirmation dialog (MainWindowViewModel.BuildRunConfirmation) tells them exactly that will happen. When the source is locked by another process, the archive folder is full, or the shell Recycle Bin call fails, the activity row still shows a green Succeeded and the status bar's LastError is cleared — the only trace is a line in the service log file. The user believes the sources were disposed of; they were not, and the next trigger will copy the same file again. The audit half is worse in the opposite direction: a PermanentDelete whose audit append fails has destroyed the file and lost the only record of it, and the spec-declared "no-loss safety net" reports success. `grep DispositionError` returns exactly three production sites — the writer, the record definition, and CrashRecovery; nothing ever reads it back.

**Proposed change.** 1) In src/FileManager.Core/Jobs/Job.cs add an init-only property to the JobCompletion record alongside ResidualPaths (line 252): `public string? DispositionError { get; init; }`. 2) In src/FileManager.Core/Jobs/JobExecutor.cs line 237, return `Completed(plan, JobOutcome.Succeeded, null, null, start) with { DispositionError = dispositionError }`. 3) In src/FileManager.Core/Jobs/JobOrchestrator.cs PublishCompletion (line 223 else-branch), before clearing _lastError, add: if `completion.DispositionError is { } de`, set `_lastError = de;` (do not clear) and `eventBus.Publish(new EngineWarningEvent { AtUtc = now, Message = $"{plan.Source.Path}: copied successfully, but the source disposition did not complete — {de}" });` — EngineWarningEvent is an existing wire type already routed by MainWindowViewModel.HandleEngineEvent (line 342) to the activity notice bar, so no protocol change is needed. 4) In src/FileManager.Core/Disposition/SourceDispositionService.cs Record (line 118), when `audit.Append` fails, return the failure to the caller as part of the disposition outcome — change Record to return `Result<DispositionAuditRecord, JobError>` and return `Failure(sourcePath, $"{action} completed but the audit record could not be written: {auditError}")` so the same channel reports it. Do NOT add a JobOutcome member: JobOutcome is serialized as an integer into the journal and stringified onto the wire.

**Blast radius.** 3 files, 4 call sites.

Job.cs (record), JobExecutor.cs (1 return site + Record's 4 call sites inside SourceDispositionService), JobOrchestrator.cs (1 publish site). JobCompletion appears 100 times across src and tests but all as a consumed value; the new property is additive and init-only, mirroring ResidualPaths. tests/FileManager.Core.Tests/Jobs/JobExecutorDispositionTests.cs:101 already asserts closed.DispositionError is non-null and gives a ready-made fixture.

**Verification.** Extend the existing disposition-failure test in tests/FileManager.Core.Tests/Jobs/JobExecutorDispositionTests.cs (the one asserting closed.DispositionError at line 101) to also assert `completion.DispositionError` is non-null. Add a JobOrchestrator test using the existing FakeJobExecutor in tests/FileManager.Core.Tests/TestSupport/Fakes.cs returning a Succeeded JobCompletion with DispositionError set, and assert an EngineWarningEvent was published and GetStatus().LastError is non-null. Existing JobExecutor* suites must stay green — Outcome remains Succeeded.

**Verifier note.** Confirmed at every cited line: JobExecutor.cs:225-228 captures dispositionError into the job-closed journal record and the per-job log, then :237 returns `Completed(plan, JobOutcome.Succeeded, null, null, start)` with a null Error; JobCompletion (Job.cs:245-253) has no field to carry it; JobOrchestrator.cs:229 clears _lastError and publishes JobCompletedEvent on that path; SourceDispositionService.Record logs the audit-append failure with the in-source comment 'audit failure never blocks disposition'. This is the batch's strongest finding: OnSuccess disposition is a user-facing promise (the run confirmation names it explicitly), and a failed MoveToTrash / MoveToArchive / PermanentDelete currently paints a green Succeeded row and clears the status bar's health hint. The remedy is proportionate and respects the frozen surface — it explicitly refuses to add a JobOutcome member (int-serialized into the journal, stringified onto the wire) and reuses the existing EngineWarningEvent, so no protocol bump. Keep at high. One caution for the executor: step 4 (changing Record to return Result<..., JobError>) widens the blast radius the most and must NOT turn a successful copy+disposition into a failed job — with step 3 in place an audit-write failure should surface as the same warning channel, not as JobOutcome.Failed.

The TreeSource-disposal memory-leak fix at :1201 and :1656 is duplicated comment-for-comment, and the rebuild-gate/debounce concurrency code is duplicated too. Downgraded from high to medium because the proposal itself is unsure whether the CommunityToolkit generator emits [ObservableProperty] partial properties on a generic abstract partial base, and hedges with 'if any fails to generate, keep that one on the derived classes' — a half-migrated base would be worse than the duplication. PREREQUISITE before executing: a throwaway spike proving (a) CTK 8.4.2 generates the observable properties and NotifyPropertyChangedFor on `DryRunTabBase<TRow>`, and (b) DryRunView.axaml's compiled bindings still resolve the inherited members with x:DataType pointing at the concrete tab types. If either fails, drop the finding rather than partially applying it.

#### `ipc-handler-list-written-twice` — All 17 IPC handler types are listed twice in Program.cs with nothing linking the two lists

| | |
|---|---|
| Lens | duplication |
| Severity | medium (verifier verdict: keep) |
| Confidence | high |
| Effort | trivial |
| Risk flags | changes-behavior |

**Claim.** src/FileManager.Service/Program.cs names each handler type once at lines 119-135 (`services.AddSingleton<XHandler>()`) and again at lines 140-156 (`provider.GetRequiredService<XHandler>()`) inside the factory that builds the dispatch dictionary. The two 17-entry lists are verbatim copies differing only in the call wrapping each name. Nothing — no test, no compiler check — ties them together; the DO-NOT-BREAK register already flags that a handler present in the DI list but absent from the table silently answers NOT_IMPLEMENTED.

**Evidence.**

- `src/FileManager.Service/Program.cs:119`

  ```csharp
  services.AddSingleton<GetStatusHandler>();
  services.AddSingleton<GetMatchingProfilesHandler>();
  services.AddSingleton<RunProfileHandler>();
  ... 14 more
  ```

- `src/FileManager.Service/Program.cs:140`

  ```csharp
      provider.GetRequiredService<GetStatusHandler>(),
      provider.GetRequiredService<GetMatchingProfilesHandler>(),
      provider.GetRequiredService<RunProfileHandler>(),
  ... the same 17 names again
  ```

- `src/FileManager.Core/IPC/IpcServer.cs:22`

  ```csharp
  IReadOnlyDictionary<string, IIpcRequestHandler> handlers) : IIpcServer
  ```


**Why it matters.** Adding a handler already requires four coordinated edits (the [JsonDerivedType] attribute, IpcRequestTypes' const + switch, the handler's RequestType, and Program.cs). This makes it five, and the fifth failure mode is the silent one: register the singleton, forget the array entry, and the service builds, starts, and answers NOT_IMPLEMENTED at runtime. IpcRequestTypesTests pins the attribute↔const pair; nothing pins this pair. It is the only un-guarded link in the chain and it is pure copy-paste.

**Proposed change.** In src/FileManager.Service/Program.cs replace each `services.AddSingleton<XHandler>();` (lines 119-135) with `services.AddSingleton<IIpcRequestHandler, XHandler>();`, then replace the whole `AddSingleton<IReadOnlyDictionary<string, IIpcRequestHandler>>(provider => { ... })` factory (lines 136-162) with:

```csharp
services.AddSingleton<IReadOnlyDictionary<string, IIpcRequestHandler>>(provider =>
{
    Dictionary<string, IIpcRequestHandler> table = new(StringComparer.Ordinal);
    foreach (IIpcRequestHandler handler in provider.GetServices<IIpcRequestHandler>())
        table.Add(handler.RequestType, handler);   // Add, not [], so a duplicate RequestType throws at startup
    return table;
});
```

This is DI enumeration of explicit registrations, not assembly scanning or reflection — it stays within the §1 AOT constraint (`GetServices<T>` over concrete registered types is AOT-safe and needs `using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection;`, already imported). Verify first that no handler is resolved by its concrete type elsewhere: I grepped src/FileManager.Service and src/FileManager.Core/IPC and found none (IpcServer takes only the dictionary; EngineHost references no handler type).

**Blast radius.** 1 file, 34 call sites.

17 AddSingleton lines + 17 GetRequiredService lines, all in Program.cs:119-156. No other file resolves a handler by concrete type (verified by grep over src/FileManager.Service and src/FileManager.Core/IPC).

**Verification.** tests/FileManager.Service.Tests/EndToEndSmokeTests.cs drives profile lifecycle, dry run, a real run, pause/resume and settings through the real pipe — every discriminator that has a handler must still answer. tests/FileManager.Core.Tests/IPC/IpcRequestTypesTests.cs still pins the attribute↔const half. Behavior change to confirm deliberately: a duplicate RequestType now throws at host build instead of being silently overwritten — that is the intent.

**Verifier note.** Verified verbatim: Program.cs:119-135 lists all 17 handler types, :140-156 lists the identical 17 again inside the dictionary factory. I confirmed the precondition the finding claims to have checked — no handler is resolved by concrete type anywhere else in src/ (IpcServer takes only the dictionary and casts to IIpcStreamingRequestHandler off the dictionary value; EngineHost names no handler). GetServices<T> over explicit registrations is AOT-safe and does not violate the §1 no-scanning rule. One-file change, deletes 17 lines of copy-paste, and closes the only unguarded link in the four-table handler chain that IpcRequestTypesTests does not cover. Minor overstatement to correct in execution: the claimed behavior change is already the current behavior — line 160 already uses `table.Add`, so a duplicate RequestType throws today too.

#### `staged-replace-fallback-duplicated` — The File.Replace → two-step-move fallback for staged overwrites is implemented twice, and the copies have already diverged

| | |
|---|---|
| Lens | duplication |
| Severity | medium (verifier verdict: keep) |
| Confidence | medium |
| Effort | small |
| Risk flags | changes-behavior, perf-sensitive |

**Claim.** AtomicPlacer.ReplaceWithStaging/TwoStepReplace (Placement/AtomicPlacer.cs:343-372) and CrashRecovery.Replace (Journal/CrashRecovery.cs:470-485) implement the same operation — move temp into final while parking the prior version at staged, falling back to a two-step move when File.Replace is rejected — with the same three-exception filter (IOException, UnauthorizedAccessException, PlatformNotSupportedException) and the same log message. They have already drifted: AtomicPlacer's fallback guards with `if (File.Exists(finalPath))` and creates the staged directory, and its doc explains this idempotency is required so a retry cannot strand the final name absent; CrashRecovery's fallback does an unguarded `File.Move(final, staged); File.Move(temp, final);`.

**Evidence.**

- `src/FileManager.Core/Placement/AtomicPlacer.cs:364`

  ```csharp
  private static void TwoStepReplace(string tempPath, string finalPath, string stagedPath)
  {
      if (File.Exists(finalPath))
      {
          Directory.CreateDirectory(Path.GetDirectoryName(stagedPath)!);
          File.Move(finalPath, stagedPath, overwrite: false);
      }
      File.Move(tempPath, finalPath, overwrite: false);
  }
  ```

- `src/FileManager.Core/Journal/CrashRecovery.cs:470`

  ```csharp
  private void Replace(string temp, string final, string staged)
  {
      try { File.Replace(temp, final, staged, ignoreMetadataErrors: true); }
      catch (Exception ex) when (ex is IOException or UnauthorizedAccessException or PlatformNotSupportedException)
      {
          logger.LogWarning(ex, "File.Replace rejected for \"{Final}\" during recovery; falling back to two-step move", final);
          File.Move(final, staged);
          File.Move(temp, final);
      }
  ```

- `src/FileManager.Core/Placement/AtomicPlacer.cs:352`

  ```csharp
  catch (Exception ex) when (ex is IOException or UnauthorizedAccessException or PlatformNotSupportedException)
  {
      // Fallback for volumes that reject ReplaceFile (some SMB servers): journaled two-step.
      logger.LogWarning(ex, "File.Replace rejected for {Final}; falling back to two-step move", finalPath);
      TwoStepReplace(tempPath, finalPath, stagedPath);
  }
  ```


**Why it matters.** This is the single most safety-critical write in the product: it is where a user's existing file is swapped for a new one while the prior version is preserved for rollback. The knowledge encoded here — which exceptions mean 'this volume rejects ReplaceFile', and that the fallback must be re-runnable — is one rule with one reason to change (a new filesystem/SMB behavior), yet it lives in two places and the second copy is missing the re-runnability property the first one's doc comment says is mandatory. Recovery re-runs the same journal rows on every startup, so a recovery pass that dies between CrashRecovery's two File.Move calls leaves the final name absent and the next pass throws FileNotFound on `File.Move(final, staged)` — exactly the stranded state AtomicPlacer's guard was written to prevent.

**Proposed change.** Add src/FileManager.Core/Files/StagedReplace.cs:

```csharp
namespace FileManager.Core.Files;

/// <summary>The staged-overwrite primitive (§4.3, I-PRIOR): swap <paramref name="tempPath"/> into
/// <paramref name="finalPath"/> while the prior version lands at <paramref name="stagedPath"/>.
/// One Win32 ReplaceFile when the volume supports it; otherwise an IDEMPOTENT two-step move so a
/// retry (live placer) or a re-run (crash recovery) after a partial attempt still completes.</summary>
internal static class StagedReplace
{
    public static void Execute(string tempPath, string finalPath, string stagedPath, ILogger logger)
    {
        try { File.Replace(tempPath, finalPath, stagedPath, ignoreMetadataErrors: true); }
        catch (Exception ex) when (ex is IOException or UnauthorizedAccessException or PlatformNotSupportedException)
        {
            logger.LogWarning(ex, "File.Replace rejected for {Final}; falling back to two-step move", finalPath);
            if (File.Exists(finalPath))
            {
                Directory.CreateDirectory(Path.GetDirectoryName(stagedPath)!);
                File.Move(finalPath, stagedPath, overwrite: false);
            }
            File.Move(tempPath, finalPath, overwrite: false);
        }
    }
}
```

Delete AtomicPlacer.ReplaceWithStaging and AtomicPlacer.TwoStepReplace; at AtomicPlacer.cs:310 call `StagedReplace.Execute(tempPath, finalPath, stagedPath, logger);`. In CrashRecovery replace the body of `Replace` (:470) with a call to `StagedReplace.Execute(temp, final, staged, logger);` inside the existing outer try that keeps its `LogError`+rethrow catch-all (:479-485) — that catch-all is recovery-specific and must stay. Do NOT fold in RollbackExecutor.TryReplace (Journal/RollbackExecutor.cs:287): it replaces in the opposite direction (staged → final) with `destinationBackupFileName: null` and an overwrite:true fallback, a genuinely different operation.

**Blast radius.** 3 files, 2 call sites.

Call sites: src/FileManager.Core/Placement/AtomicPlacer.cs:310 and src/FileManager.Core/Journal/CrashRecovery.cs:274. New file src/FileManager.Core/Files/StagedReplace.cs. RollbackExecutor.cs:287 deliberately excluded.

**Verification.** tests/FileManager.Core.Tests/Placement/AtomicPlacerTests.cs (staged-replace placement) and tests/FileManager.Core.Tests/Journal/CrashRecoveryTests.cs (the hand-authored post-crash journal + on-disk state matrix) both cover these paths. Add one CrashRecovery test for the pre-moved-prior state: journal rows for a StageOverwrites target, final absent, staged already present, temp present — recovery must complete the placement rather than throw. That case fails on today's code and passes after the change.

**Verifier note.** Best finding in the batch. Verified exactly: AtomicPlacer.cs:364-372 guards the fallback with File.Exists(finalPath) and documents that idempotency as mandatory ('a retry after the first move succeeded but the second failed would throw FileNotFound forever and strand the final name absent'), while CrashRecovery.cs:476-477 does the same two moves unguarded — and CrashRecovery.Replace is called from the recovery replay path (CrashRecovery.cs:274), which re-runs the same journal rows on every service start. That is a real latent data-stranding bug in the most safety-critical write in the product, not a tidiness complaint. Scope is small (3 files, 2 call sites), the exclusion of RollbackExecutor.TryReplace is correctly reasoned (opposite direction, null backup, overwrite:true), and the proposed new CrashRecoveryTests case fails today and passes after — which satisfies the characterization-test bar. Keep the recovery-specific LogError+rethrow catch-all in place as the finding says.

#### `settings-static-defaults-override-injected-enginepaths` — Two engine directories resolve from a static Contracts default, silently overriding the injected EnginePaths root

| | |
|---|---|
| Lens | layering-dependencies |
| Severity | medium (verifier verdict: downgrade) |
| Confidence | high |
| Effort | small |
| Risk flags | changes-behavior, wide-blast-radius |

**Claim.** GlobalSettings.ProfilesDirectory and .ScratchDirectory fall back to process-global static properties that hardcode %LOCALAPPDATA%\FileManager, and SettingsService returns those defaults without rebasing them on the EnginePaths it was injected with. Every other engine directory is Root-relative and injectable; these two are not, so pointing EnginePaths.Root at a temp directory silently leaves the profile store and dry-run spool aimed at the developer's real user data.

**Evidence.**

- `src/FileManager.Core/Settings/SettingsService.cs:86`

  ```csharp
  if (!File.Exists(file))
      return GlobalSettings.Default;   // _paths is injected but never consulted for directory defaults
  ```

- `src/FileManager.Contracts/Settings/GlobalSettings.cs:91`

  ```csharp
  get => _profilesDirectory ?? DefaultProfilesDirectory;   // static: %LOCALAPPDATA%\FileManager\profiles
  ```

- `src/FileManager.Core/Profiles/ProfileStore.cs:25`

  ```csharp
  private string ProfilesDirectory => settings.Current.ProfilesDirectory;
  ```

- `src/FileManager.Service/EngineHost.cs:75`

  ```csharp
  Directory.CreateDirectory(paths.ProfilesDirectory);   // creates <Root>\profiles, which ProfileStore never reads
  ```

- `tests/FileManager.Service.Tests/EndToEndSmokeTests.cs:70`

  ```csharp
  settings.Update(settings.Current with { ProfilesDirectory = Path.Combine(paths.Root, "profiles") });
  ```


**Why it matters.** The injectable-root seam does not actually cover the two directories that hold user data. EngineHost creates <Root>\profiles and then ProfileStore reads a different directory entirely. The end-to-end smoke test has a hand-written pin at EndToEndSmokeTests.cs:70 with a comment explaining it exists "so the smoke test never touches the real %LOCALAPPDATA% profiles directory" — a workaround every future harness must remember and that nothing enforces. ScratchDirectory has no such pin at all, so a spilling dry run in that test writes into the developer's real %LOCALAPPDATA%\FileManager\scratch. Forgetting the pin is a silent data-touching bug, not a test failure.

**Proposed change.** 1. Add to src/FileManager.Core/EnginePaths.cs: `public string ScratchDirectory => Path.Combine(Root, "scratch");` (beside the existing ProfilesDirectory/LogsDirectory members). 2. In src/FileManager.Core/Settings/SettingsService.cs add a private method `private GlobalSettings Rebase(GlobalSettings s) => s with { ProfilesDirectory = s.ProfilesDirectorySerialized ?? _paths.ProfilesDirectory, ScratchDirectory = s.ScratchDirectorySerialized ?? _paths.ScratchDirectory };` and apply it to every value returned from Load() — both `return GlobalSettings.Default;` branches (lines 86, 93, 100, 106) and the `return Normalize(MigrateLegacy(...))` at line 95. Use the `…Serialized` shadow properties, not the resolved getters, so only ABSENT values are rebased and an explicitly-configured directory is left alone. 3. Do NOT modify GlobalSettings — it is frozen; its collapse-to-null init logic still compares against the static defaults, so when Root is the production %LOCALAPPDATA%\FileManager the rebased value equals DefaultProfilesDirectory/DefaultScratchDirectory and collapses straight back to null: settings.json stays byte-identical. 4. Delete the manual pin at tests/FileManager.Service.Tests/EndToEndSmokeTests.cs:68-70. 5. Update tests/FileManager.Core.Tests/Settings/SettingsServiceTests.cs:163 and :178, which assert against `GlobalSettings.Default` / `GlobalSettings.Default.ScratchDirectory`; under a temp root they must now expect `_paths.ProfilesDirectory` / `_paths.ScratchDirectory`.

**Blast radius.** 4 files, 4 call sites.

Only four reads of the two properties exist across src/: ProfileStore.cs:25, RelocateProfilesHandler.cs:45, DryRunEngine.cs:118, EngineHost.cs:175. Production behavior is unchanged because EnginePaths.Default().Root already equals the static defaults' parent; only injected-root callers (tests, harnesses) change. Two existing assertions in SettingsServiceTests must be updated.

**Verification.** Run tests/FileManager.Core.Tests/Settings/SettingsServiceTests.cs and confirm Unset_directories_stay_absent_through_an_update_round_trip still shows ScratchDirectory/ProfilesDirectory absent-or-null in the written settings.json (this is the proof the on-disk format is unchanged). Then delete the EndToEndSmokeTests.cs:70 pin and confirm the suite still passes AND that %LOCALAPPDATA%\FileManager\profiles is not created/modified during the run.

**Verifier note.** All four citations verified (SettingsService.cs:86 returns GlobalSettings.Default without consulting the injected _paths; GlobalSettings.cs:91 resolves from the static default; EngineHost.cs:75 creates <Root>\profiles; the EndToEndSmokeTests.cs:70 pin and its comment exist verbatim). But the severity is wrong: Program.cs:42 is the only production construction and it passes EnginePaths.Default(), whose Root IS %LOCALAPPDATA%\FileManager — the same base the two static defaults resolve against. So there is no production divergence; the concrete harm is test isolation (a spilling dry run in the smoke test writing into the developer's real %LOCALAPPDATA%\FileManager\scratch, since ScratchDirectory has no pin at all, and EngineHost's PurgeScratchDirectory sweeping it). That is worth fixing, at medium. Two execution prerequisites the finding is thin on: (1) Rebase must be applied AFTER Normalize (SettingsService.cs:152-157 re-resolves both directories against the static defaults, so Rebase(Normalize(x)) is the only correct ordering); (2) the SettingsServiceTests round-trip that proves settings.json stays byte-identical (unset directories absent) is the gate — if it goes red, stop, because the on-disk shape is frozen.

#### `dryrun-row-commands-no-shared-contract` — Three dry-run row types share five command names by comment convention only — no interface, and the bindings are reflection-resolved

| | |
|---|---|
| Lens | divergent-parallel-modules |
| Severity | medium (verifier verdict: keep) |
| Confidence | high |
| Effort | small |
| Risk flags | markup-binding-adjacent, touches-generated-code |

**Claim.** DryRunFileRow, DryRunDestinationRow and DryRunTreeNode each independently declare CopyPathCommand / CopyNameCommand / CopyNameWithoutExtensionCommand / OpenFileCommand / RevealInExplorerCommand. Nothing in the type system relates them. One shared MenuFlyout (FileContextMenu) is applied to both flat-list row types inside an x:CompileBindings="False" region, so every one of those bindings is resolved by reflection at runtime, and the view code-behind reaches the members through two hand-written type switches instead of a common type.

**Evidence.**

- `src/FileManager.UI/ViewModels/DryRunViewModel.cs:66`

  ```csharp
  public IRelayCommand CopyPathCommand => new RelayCommand(() => Actions?.CopyText(SourcePath));   // preceded by: "Names mirror DryRunTreeNode so the shared file menu markup binds the same command names on either type."
  ```

- `src/FileManager.UI/ViewModels/DryRunViewModel.cs:266`

  ```csharp
  public IRelayCommand CopyPathCommand => new RelayCommand(() => Actions?.CopyText(Primary.TargetPath));   // preceded by: "Names mirror the tree node / source row so the shared file menu markup binds identically."
  ```

- `src/FileManager.UI/ViewModels/DryRunViewModel.cs:501`

  ```csharp
  [RelayCommand] private void CopyPath() => _controller?.Actions?.CopyText(FullPath);
  ```

- `src/FileManager.UI/Views/DryRunView.axaml:111`

  ```csharp
  <MenuFlyout x:Key="FileContextMenu" x:CompileBindings="False"> ... Command="{Binding CopyPathCommand}"   (applied at lines 462 and 600 to two different row types)
  ```

- `src/FileManager.UI/Views/DryRunView.axaml.cs:161`

  ```csharp
  case DryRunFileRow r:
      (copyPath, copyName, openFile, reveal) = (r.CopyPathCommand, r.CopyNameCommand, r.OpenFileCommand, r.RevealInExplorerCommand);
      break;
  case DryRunDestinationRow r:
      (copyPath, copyName, openFile, reveal) = (r.CopyPathCommand, r.CopyNameCommand, r.OpenFileCommand, r.RevealInExplorerCommand);
  ```


**Why it matters.** Renaming or removing one of these five members on one row type — including indirectly, by renaming a [RelayCommand] method on DryRunTreeNode, which changes the generated command name — compiles cleanly, passes the XAML compile (the flyouts opt out of compiled bindings), and produces a dead right-click menu item for exactly one of the three row kinds at runtime. The only thing holding the three in step today is a comment on each type telling the reader to mirror the others. The same code-behind duplication is written twice (lines 65-70 and 161-170) purely to reach identically-named members through no common type.

**Proposed change.** Add to src/FileManager.UI/ViewModels/DryRunViewModel.cs (or a new src/FileManager.UI/ViewModels/IDryRunFileRow.cs):

    public interface IDryRunFileRow
    {
        IRelayCommand CopyPathCommand { get; }
        IRelayCommand CopyNameCommand { get; }
        IRelayCommand CopyNameWithoutExtensionCommand { get; }
        IRelayCommand OpenFileCommand { get; }
        IRelayCommand RevealInExplorerCommand { get; }
    }

Declare `DryRunFileRow`, `DryRunDestinationRow` and `DryRunTreeNode` as implementing it (all five members already exist with matching names and IRelayCommand type — DryRunTreeNode's are the CommunityToolkit-generated properties for CopyPath/CopyName/CopyNameWithoutExtension/OpenFile/RevealInExplorer, so no member bodies change). Do NOT add the folder-only OpenFolderInExplorerCommand to the interface; it exists on DryRunTreeNode only, which is a genuine domain difference.

Then collapse the two type switches in src/FileManager.UI/Views/DryRunView.axaml.cs: at line 65 replace the `dataContext switch { DryRunFileRow row => ..., DryRunDestinationRow row => ..., _ => null }` with `dataContext is IDryRunFileRow row ? row.OpenFileCommand : null`; at line 161 replace the `switch (item)` block with `if (item is not IDryRunFileRow r) return;` followed by direct member access.

Leave the XAML flyouts as-is (they must stay x:CompileBindings="False" — one flyout serves two unrelated DataContext types). The interface is the compile-time guarantee that both types keep the members the flyout names.

**Blast radius.** 3 files, 9 call sites.

Counted: 3 declaration sites in src/FileManager.UI/ViewModels/DryRunViewModel.cs (lines 44, 250, 351); 2 type switches in src/FileManager.UI/Views/DryRunView.axaml.cs (lines 65, 161); 1 shared MenuFlyout in DryRunView.axaml (line 111) referenced at lines 462 and 600; 1 node flyout at line 62; 5 command assertions in tests/FileManager.UI.Tests/DryRunItemActionsCommandsTests.cs, which continue to compile unchanged.

**Verification.** Build the UI project (the interface is purely additive; any member-name drift on one of the three types now fails the compile). Run tests/FileManager.UI.Tests/DryRunItemActionsCommandsTests.cs and DryRunViewSmokeTests. Manually right-click a row in the Sources list, the Destinations list, and a file node in the tree and confirm all five menu items still act.

**Verifier note.** Verified precisely: all five command names exist as IRelayCommand on DryRunFileRow (:66-76), DryRunDestinationRow (:266-275) and as [RelayCommand]-generated properties on DryRunTreeNode (:501-510); DryRunView.axaml:111 is an x:CompileBindings="False" flyout shared by two row types; the code-behind reaches them through hand-written type switches at :65 and :161 with comments ('both row types expose the same command names') that are the only thing holding the three in step. A purely additive marker interface converts a runtime-silent break — a dead right-click item on exactly one row kind, invisible to the XAML compile because the region opts out of compiled bindings — into a build error, at the cost of three type-declaration edits and collapsing two switches. That is the cheapest possible guard for the reflection-bound surface the constraints register explicitly calls out as public API. Severity lowered to medium (worst case is a dead menu item, not data loss); correctly excludes OpenFolderInExplorerCommand, which is folder-only.

#### `catalog-reload-failure-three-semantics` — The three catalog-mutating IPC handlers give three different answers to the same failed catalog reload

| | |
|---|---|
| Lens | divergent-parallel-modules |
| Severity | medium (verifier verdict: keep) |
| Confidence | high |
| Effort | small |
| Risk flags | changes-behavior, no-test-coverage |

**Claim.** SaveProfileHandler, DeleteProfileHandler and RelocateProfilesHandler all mutate profiles on disk and then call catalog.Reload(). RelocateProfilesHandler treats a reload failure as an ErrorResponse with a documented rationale; SaveProfileHandler and DeleteProfileHandler log a warning and report success. ProfileCatalog.Reload returns early on failure without swapping the snapshot and without notifying subscribers, so on that path the service keeps serving the pre-mutation profile set and no ProfilesChangedEvent is broadcast — while the client is told the operation succeeded.

**Evidence.**

- `src/FileManager.Core/IPC/Handlers/SaveProfileHandler.cs:31`

  ```csharp
  Result reload = catalog.Reload();
  if (reload.TryGetError(out string? reloadError))
      logger.LogWarning("Catalog reload after save failed: {Error}", reloadError);
  
  IpcResponse response = new ValidationResponse { Issues = issues! };
  ```

- `src/FileManager.Core/IPC/Handlers/DeleteProfileHandler.cs:25`

  ```csharp
  Result reload = catalog.Reload();
  if (reload.TryGetError(out string? reloadError))
      logger.LogWarning("Catalog reload after delete failed: {Error}", reloadError);
  
  IpcResponse response = new OkResponse();
  ```

- `src/FileManager.Core/IPC/Handlers/RelocateProfilesHandler.cs:122`

  ```csharp
  var reload = catalog.Reload();
  if (reload.TryGetError(out string? reloadError))
  {
      logger.LogError("Catalog reload after relocation failed: {Error}", reloadError);
      return Fail("PROFILES_RELOCATE_FAILED", $"the profiles directory was changed to \"{newDir}\", but reloading the profiles failed: {reloadError}; retry, or restart the service");
  ```

- `src/FileManager.Core/Profiles/ProfileCatalog.cs:38`

  ```csharp
  if (loaded.TryGetError(out string? error))
      return error;      // snapshot not swapped, _subscribers.Notify never reached
  ```

- `src/FileManager.Core/IPC/Handlers/RunProfileHandler.cs:41`

  ```csharp
  Profile? profile = catalog.All.FirstOrDefault(p => p.Id == typed.ProfileId);
  ```


**Why it matters.** RelocateProfilesHandler's own comment states the reason a reload failure must not report success — "the catalog would keep serving the old directory's snapshot until some later reload" — and that reason applies verbatim to save and delete. After a swallowed reload failure the engine keeps executing the stale profile: RunProfileHandler resolves from catalog.All, so a manual run enqueues a job under the pre-save policy, including a stale OnSuccessAction that can be PermanentDelete. Deleting a profile the user just deleted still runs. Neither the requesting client nor any other subscriber learns anything, because the ProfilesChangedEvent bridge (src/FileManager.Service/EngineHost.cs:141) only fires from a successful reload.

**Proposed change.** Give the three handlers one rule. Add src/FileManager.Core/IPC/Handlers/CatalogReloadGuard.cs:

    internal static class CatalogReloadGuard
    {
        /// Returns null when the reload succeeded, else the ErrorResponse the handler must return.
        public static ErrorResponse? Check(IProfileCatalog catalog, ILogger logger, string code, string didWhat)
        {
            Result reload = catalog.Reload();
            if (!reload.TryGetError(out string? error)) return null;
            logger.LogError("Catalog reload after {DidWhat} failed: {Error}", didWhat, error);
            return new ErrorResponse { Code = code, Message = $"the profile was {didWhat}, but reloading the profile list failed: {error}; retry, or restart the service" };
        }
    }

In SaveProfileHandler.HandleAsync replace lines 31-33 with `if (CatalogReloadGuard.Check(catalog, logger, "PROFILE_SAVE_FAILED", "saved") is { } failure) return Task.FromResult<IpcResponse>(failure);`. In DeleteProfileHandler replace lines 25-27 with the same call using "PROFILE_DELETE_FAILED" / "deleted". In RelocateProfilesHandler replace lines 122-129 with the call using "PROFILES_RELOCATE_FAILED" / $"relocated to \"{newDir}\"" so all three share one definition.

The UI already handles an ErrorResponse on both routes (IpcGateway.SaveProfileAsync at src/FileManager.UI/Services/IpcGateway.cs:48 and DeleteProfileAsync at line 58 both surface IpcError), so no client change is needed. Reuse the existing PROFILE_SAVE_FAILED / PROFILE_DELETE_FAILED codes rather than inventing new ones — the UI matches neither by string, it only displays the message.

**Blast radius.** 4 files, 3 call sites.

Three catalog.Reload() call sites in src/FileManager.Core/IPC/Handlers/ (SaveProfileHandler.cs:31, DeleteProfileHandler.cs:25, RelocateProfilesHandler.cs:122) plus one new file. The fourth Reload() in the repo, EngineHost.cs:91, is the startup load and is deliberately non-fatal — leave it.

**Verification.** tests/FileManager.Core.Tests/IPC/RelocateProfilesHandlerTests.cs already pins the relocate branch — it must stay green. SaveProfileHandler and DeleteProfileHandler have no dedicated test (their only exercise is tests/FileManager.Service.Tests/EndToEndSmokeTests.cs:106-122), so add two direct handler tests with an IProfileCatalog double whose Reload() returns a failure, asserting an ErrorResponse rather than ValidationResponse/OkResponse. Then run EndToEndSmokeTests to confirm the happy path is unchanged.

**Verifier note.** All five citations check out verbatim: SaveProfileHandler.cs:31-33 and DeleteProfileHandler.cs:25-27 log-and-report-success, RelocateProfilesHandler.cs:122-129 fails loud with a comment stating precisely why ('the catalog would keep serving the old directory's snapshot'), and ProfileCatalog.Reload returns early without swapping _snapshot or calling _subscribers.Notify. So on that path the service serves a stale catalog, broadcasts no ProfilesChangedEvent, and tells the client OK — and RunProfileHandler.cs:41 resolves the job's profile from that stale catalog.All, including a stale OnSuccessAction. Genuine inconsistency on a destructive path, three small handlers, one shared guard, existing UI error routes need no change, and the finding correctly declines to invent new error codes. Kept at medium rather than raised: ProfileStore.LoadAll fails soft per-profile, so Reload only errors on a directory-level fault — rare. Two nits for the executor: the shared message template reads awkwardly for the relocate case ('the profile was relocated to "..."'), so keep relocate's existing wording; and a save that DID reach disk now returns ErrorResponse, so the message must say so plainly.

#### `startup-catalog-load-failure-serves-empty-profile-list` — A failed profile load at startup is logged and the engine proceeds with an empty catalog, so the UI shows zero profiles indistinguishably from "you have none"

| | |
|---|---|
| Lens | error-handling-failure-modes |
| Severity | medium (verifier verdict: downgrade) |
| Confidence | high |
| Effort | trivial |
| Risk flags | no-test-coverage |

**Claim.** EngineHost logs an error when catalog.Reload() fails and continues the startup sequence. ProfileCatalog leaves its snapshot at the initial empty pair, and ListProfilesHandler serves catalog.All directly, so list-profiles returns an empty successful ProfileListResponse. JobOrchestrator then drops every incoming payload with an Information-level "profile no longer exists".

**Evidence.**

- `src/FileManager.Service/EngineHost.cs:91`

  ```csharp
  Result reload = catalog.Reload();
  if (reload.TryGetError(out string? reloadError))
      logger.LogError("Initial profile load failed: {Error}", reloadError);
  ```

- `src/FileManager.Core/Profiles/ProfileCatalog.cs:37`

  ```csharp
  Result<IReadOnlyList<Profile>, string> loaded = store.LoadAll();
  if (loaded.TryGetError(out string? error))
      return error;   // _snapshot is left at new([], [])
  ```

- `src/FileManager.Core/IPC/Handlers/ListProfilesHandler.cs:17`

  ```csharp
  foreach (Profile profile in catalog.All)
      summaries.Add(new ProfileSummary(profile.Id, profile.Name, profile.Active, TriggerSummary(profile)));
  ```

- `src/FileManager.Core/Jobs/JobOrchestrator.cs:135`

  ```csharp
  if (profile is null)
  {
      logger.LogInformation("Dropping payload for {SourcePath}: profile {ProfileId} no longer exists", ...);
      return;
  }
  ```


**Why it matters.** LoadAll returns an error whenever the profiles directory cannot be enumerated — a relocated ProfilesDirectory on a network share that is not mounted yet at logon (the service autostarts from HKCU Run, before drives may be connected) or a permissions change. The user opens the app and sees an empty profile list, no banner, no warning; the status bar reports a healthy connected engine with ActiveProfiles: 0. Every watcher/manual trigger is then dropped at Information level. The natural user response is to re-create the profiles, which duplicates them once the directory comes back. The service already holds IEngineEventBus and the wire already has an EngineWarningEvent that the UI renders in the activity notice bar — the failure just is not put on it.

**Proposed change.** In src/FileManager.Service/EngineHost.cs, capture the reload error: replace the block at lines 91-93 with `Result reload = catalog.Reload(); string? profileLoadError = reload.TryGetError(out string? e) ? e : null; if (profileLoadError is not null) logger.LogError("Initial profile load failed: {Error}", profileLoadError);`. Then after the event bridges are wired (immediately after `_eventBridge = eventBus.Subscribe(ipcServer.Broadcast);` at line 134) add: `if (profileLoadError is not null) eventBus.Publish(new EngineWarningEvent { AtUtc = time.GetUtcNow(), Message = $"Profiles could not be loaded from {settings.Current.ProfilesDirectory}: {profileLoadError}. The profile list is empty and no triggers will run until this is fixed." });`. Publishing after the bridge is created is what makes it reach IPC subscribers; a UI connecting later re-seeds via ReconcileEngineStateAsync, so also retry catalog.Reload() on the next list-profiles is out of scope here — the warning is the fix.

**Blast radius.** 1 file, 1 call site.

EngineHost.cs only. eventBus and time are already constructor-injected (lines 32, 34); EngineWarningEvent is already handled by MainWindowViewModel.HandleEngineEvent line 342 and covered by tests/FileManager.UI.Tests/MainWindowViewModelEventRoutingTests.cs:82.

**Verification.** In tests/FileManager.Service.Tests/EndToEndSmokeTests.cs, point the engine root's profiles directory at a path that cannot be enumerated (e.g. a file where a directory is expected) before InitializeAsync, subscribe to events over the real pipe, and assert an engine-warning frame arrives. Existing smoke tests must stay green — the change only adds a publish on the error path.

**Verifier note.** The four citations are all accurate (EngineHost.cs:91-93 logs and continues; ProfileCatalog.cs:37 returns leaving _snapshot empty; ListProfilesHandler serves catalog.All; JobOrchestrator.cs:135 drops payloads at Information). But the headline scenario is wrong, and it is the scenario that carries the severity: ProfileStore.LoadAll begins `if (!Directory.Exists(ProfilesDirectory)) return Array.Empty<Profile>()` (ProfileStore.cs:31-32), so a relocated ProfilesDirectory on an unmounted network share at logon returns SUCCESS with zero profiles — the proposed EngineWarningEvent would never fire, and the user still sees the silent empty list the finding describes. Only the enumeration-throws case (permissions change, IOException, ProfileStore.cs:61-64) reaches the error path the fix hooks. Downgraded to medium, with the prerequisite that the change also cover the directory-missing case (warn when the configured ProfilesDirectory does not exist) — otherwise it fixes the narrow half and leaves the motivating failure untouched. The publish-after-_eventBridge placement is correct and must be preserved, and it must stay below the step-3 comment's load-bearing ordering note.

#### `enginehost-startup-sequence-unreachable` — The service's whole startup sequence (I-RECOVER-FIRST) has zero test coverage and cannot be constructed by a test

**Claim.** EngineHost is the only place the §2.4 startup ordering exists — crash recovery must complete before the IPC server accepts connections, and the event/pause/profile bridges must be installed after catalog.Reload() but before the orchestrator starts. It is `internal sealed` in FileManager.Service, and FileManager.Service.csproj declares no InternalsVisibleTo, so FileManager.Service.Tests (which does reference the project) cannot name the type. No test constructs it; the only mention of "EngineHost" anywhere under tests/ is a comment.

**Evidence.**

- `src/FileManager.Service/EngineHost.cs:22`

  ```csharp
  internal sealed class EngineHost(
      ILogger<EngineHost> logger,
      IHostApplicationLifetime lifetime,
      Core.EnginePaths paths,
  ```

- `src/FileManager.Service/EngineHost.cs:98`

  ```csharp
  // 4. Crash recovery — resolves every OPEN journal entry to CLOSED. MUST run to completion
  //    here, before step 5 starts the IPC server ... (I-RECOVER-FIRST, §7.4).
  Result<RecoveryReport, Core.Jobs.JobError> recovery = crashRecovery.Recover(stoppingToken);
  ```

- `src/FileManager.Service/EngineHost.cs:133`

  ```csharp
  //    These MUST stay below step 3's catalog.Reload() — creating the catalog bridge earlier
  //    would publish a spurious profiles-changed at startup. That ordering is load-bearing.
  ```

- `src/FileManager.Service/FileManager.Service.csproj:19`

  ```csharp
    <ItemGroup>
      <ProjectReference Include="..\FileManager.Contracts\FileManager.Contracts.csproj" />
  ```

- `src/FileManager.Service/EngineHost.cs:64`

  ```csharp
  _singleInstanceMutex = new Mutex(
      initiallyOwned: false,
      name: @"Local\FileManager.Service." + IpcEndpoint.SanitizeUserName(Environment.UserName));
  ```


**Why it matters.** I-RECOVER-FIRST is the invariant that keeps a crashed job's staged prior versions of the user's files recoverable: if the IPC server (or the orchestrator) starts before CrashRecovery.Recover returns, a new job can take path locks over files that recovery was about to restore. CrashRecovery itself is heavily tested (tests/FileManager.Core.Tests/Journal/CrashRecoveryTests.cs, 1085 LOC) — but nothing tests that it is *called first*. Equally, the two documented early-exit paths (recovery failure and IPC-start failure both call lifetime.StopApplication() and return) have never been executed by a test, so a regression that starts the pipeline anyway is invisible. This is also the blocking dependency for every other structural change in FileManager.Service: the composition-root extraction below cannot be verified without it.

**Proposed change.** Two edits, then one new test file.

1. Add to src/FileManager.Service/FileManager.Service.csproj, inside a new ItemGroup:
   <InternalsVisibleTo Include="FileManager.Service.Tests" />
   (matching the existing declarations in src/FileManager.Core/FileManager.Core.csproj:26 and src/FileManager.UI/FileManager.UI.csproj:18).

2. In src/FileManager.Service/EngineHost.cs, add a trailing optional constructor parameter `string? instanceMutexName = null` and change line 64-66 to use `name: instanceMutexName ?? (@"Local\FileManager.Service." + IpcEndpoint.SanitizeUserName(Environment.UserName))`. Do NOT move the derivation out of EngineHost — the literal is a frozen cross-process contract. This exists only so a test never contends with a real service running on the developer's machine.

3. Add tests/FileManager.Service.Tests/EngineHostStartupTests.cs. Construct EngineHost with NullLogger, a stub IHostApplicationLifetime that records StopApplication(), an EnginePaths pointed at a temp root, a unique instanceMutexName, TimeProvider.System, and recording fakes for IProfileCatalog / IIpcServer / ICrashRecovery / IJobOrchestrator / IEngineEventBus / IPauseStateService / IAutostartRegistrar / ISettingsProvider. Each fake appends its own name to a shared List<string> ordering log. Call StartAsync/StopAsync and assert:
   - the ordering log is exactly ["catalog.Reload", "crashRecovery.Recover", "ipcServer.Start", "eventBus.Subscribe", "pauseState.Subscribe", "catalog.Subscribe", "orchestrator.Start"] — pinning I-RECOVER-FIRST and the bridges-after-Reload rule;
   - when ICrashRecovery returns a JobError, ipcServer.Start and orchestrator.Start are never called and StopApplication was invoked;
   - when IIpcServer.Start returns an error, orchestrator.Start is never called;
   - on shutdown the order is orchestrator.StopAsync then ipcServer.StopAsync;
   - a second EngineHost sharing the same instanceMutexName exits without calling Reload/Recover/Start.

**Blast radius.** 2 files, 1 call site.

EngineHost is constructed in exactly one place: services.AddHostedService<EngineHost>() at src/FileManager.Service/Program.cs:165. The csproj edit is additive. The constructor gains an optional trailing parameter, so the DI activation at Program.cs:165 is unchanged (Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection binds the longest constructor it can satisfy; with a defaulted string it still resolves — verify by running the existing Service tests plus a manual F5).

**Verification.** Run tests/FileManager.Service.Tests (the new suite plus the existing EndToEndSmokeTests / IpcRobustnessTests / IpcServerStreamingTests, which all take PipeCollection). Then run FileManager.Service.exe once manually and confirm logs/service-YYYYMMDD.log still shows "Recovery complete" before any IPC activity — the DI-activation change to the constructor is the only production-behavior risk and it fails loudly at host build.

**Verifier note.** Evidence fully confirmed: EngineHost is internal sealed (EngineHost.cs:22), FileManager.Service.csproj has no InternalsVisibleTo (I read the whole file), and the only occurrence of "EngineHost" under tests/ is a comment at EndToEndSmokeTests.cs:129. The ordering really is load-bearing and self-documented (I-RECOVER-FIRST at :95-98, the bridges-after-Reload note at :131-133, three lifetime.StopApplication() early exits at :111, :120, :147, none exercised). Worth doing — two trivial production edits plus a test file is not churn. Downgraded from critical because nothing is broken today; this is a coverage gap, not a defect, and "critical" would push it above a live data-loss bug in the same batch. Two prerequisites: (a) assert the load-bearing ORDERING CONSTRAINTS (Reload before Recover, Recover before ipcServer.Start, bridges after Reload and before orchestrator.Start) and the three early-exit paths — do NOT assert an exact seven-string call transcript, which pins incidental order and becomes a maintenance tax; (b) confirm the optional `instanceMutexName` default is honored by ActivatorUtilities under AddHostedService before relying on it, since the DI graph fails at host build, not compile.

**Why it matters.** Two concrete costs.        Task<Result<DryRunReport, IpcError>> DryRunStreamAsync(DryRunStreamRequest request, IProgress<DryRunProgress>? progress = null, CancellationToken ct = default);
       IAsyncEnumerable<EngineEvent> SubscribeAsync(CancellationToken ct = default);
   }
   These are the exact existing public signatures of IpcClient — add `, IIpcConnection` to the declaration at src/FileManager.Contracts/IPC/IpcClient.cs:15 and change nothing else in that file. BCL-only, so it is legal in Contracts and stays AOT/trim-clean.

2. In src/FileManager.UI/Services/IpcGateway.cs: change the field at line 28 to `IIpcConnection? _client`, and add a constructor taking two delegates with production defaults:

       Func<CancellationToken, Task<Result<IIpcConnection, string>>>? connectOrStart = null,
       Func<CancellationToken, Task<Result<IIpcConnection, string>>>? connectOnly = null)
   defaulting to thin lambdas over ServiceLauncher.ConnectOrStartAsync (used at lines 173 and 287) and IpcClient.ConnectAsync (used at line 109). Keep the parameterless call site in App.axaml.cs:34 working via the defaults.

3. Add tests/FileManager.UI.Tests/IpcGatewayTests.cs with a FakeConnection : IIpcConnection that scripts per-request outcomes, an IsPoisoned flag, and a Disposed counter. Cover: the shared client is reused across two successive requests (connect delegate invoked once); an IPC_TRANSPORT / IPC_UNEXPECTED_RESPONSE / IPC_MALFORMED error disposes the client and the next request connects a fresh one; a non-transport error code (e.g. PROFILE_NOT_FOUND) does NOT drop the client; IsPoisoned after a successful-looking response still drops; DryRunAsync and SubscribeEventsAsync each take their own connection and never touch the shared one; DisposeAsync followed by a request returns an IpcError rather than throwing ObjectDisposedException.

4. In the same file, add SaveProfileAsync tests over a FakeConnection returning a scripted ValidationResponse, asserting SaveOutcome.Saved for the four combinations (Error present; BlockingWarning with acknowledgeWarnings false; BlockingWarning with acknowledgeWarnings true; Info only) — mirroring the assertions in ProfileStoreTests so drift between the two copies of the rule becomes a red test.

**Blast radius.** 3 files, 1 call site.

`new IpcGateway()` appears exactly once (App.axaml.cs:34) and keeps working via defaulted parameters. Adding `IIpcConnection` to IpcClient is purely additive: the 4 files in tests/FileManager.Service.Tests that use the concrete IpcClient (EndToEndSmokeTests, IpcRobustnessTests, IpcServerOversizedResponseTests, IpcServerStreamingTests) are unaffected. 16 files in src/FileManager.UI depend on IIpcGateway, not IpcGateway, and are untouched.

**Verification.** Existing tests/FileManager.UI.Tests must stay green unchanged (they only use IIpcGateway). Then start the service and the UI and exercise the recovery path by hand: kill FileManager.Service.exe with the UI open, confirm the status bar goes disconnected, restart the service, confirm the UI reconnects on the next 2s poll without an app restart — that is the behavior the new tests are pinning.

**Verifier note.** Every claim checks out: there is no IpcGatewayTests.cs in tests/FileManager.UI.Tests, IpcGateway.cs:28 holds a concrete IpcClient?, connections come from the statics ServiceLauncher.ConnectOrStartAsync and IpcClient.ConnectAsync, the drop rule at :248 matches three free string literals, and the SaveOutcome rule at :53 is a hand-copy of ProfileStore.cs:111 with its own comment saying so (and ProfileStoreTests.cs:83-90 tests only the service-side copy). #### `scanscheduler-worker-lifecycle-unobservable` — ScanScheduler's global thread ceiling and worker retirement cannot be asserted — _liveWorkers is private and the idle timeout is a 15-second const

| | |
|---|---|
| Lens | testability-seams |
| Severity | medium (verifier verdict: downgrade) |
| Confidence | high |
| Effort | trivial |
| Risk flags | perf-sensitive, test-flakiness |

**Claim.** ScanScheduler is the process-wide owner of every directory-enumeration thread, shared by the source scan and the destination sweep. Its five existing tests cover per-volume caps, per-session backpressure, cancellation and re-arm — none of them can observe the worker pool itself, because `_liveWorkers` is a private int with no accessor and retirement is gated on `Monitor.Wait(_lock, IdleTimeoutMs)` with `IdleTimeoutMs = 15_000` as a private const. Asserting that the global cap is honoured, that workers ramp down, or that a retired worker respawns would require a 15-second wall-clock test with no way to read the count.

**Evidence.**

- `src/FileManager.Core/Scanning/ScanScheduler.cs:32`

  ```csharp
  private const int IdleTimeoutMs = 15_000;
  ```

- `src/FileManager.Core/Scanning/ScanScheduler.cs:86`

  ```csharp
  int cap = Math.Max(1, ScanThreadResolver.ResolveMaxScanThreads(_settings.Current.ScanThreading));
  if (_liveWorkers >= cap)
      return;
  _liveWorkers++;
  Task.Factory.StartNew(WorkerLoop, CancellationToken.None, TaskCreationOptions.LongRunning, TaskScheduler.Default);
  ```

- `src/FileManager.Core/Scanning/ScanScheduler.cs:114`

  ```csharp
  if (!Monitor.Wait(_lock, IdleTimeoutMs) && !TryClaimLocked(out session, out work))
  {
      _liveWorkers--;
      return;
  }
  ```

- `tests/FileManager.Core.Tests/Scanning/ScanSchedulerTests.cs:15`

  ```csharp
  [Fact]
  public void Per_volume_cap_bounds_concurrent_enumeration()
  ... the file's five facts are Per_volume_cap / A_stalled_consumer / Cancelling_one_session / A_root_submitted_after / Submitting_a_root_after — none reference the worker count or retirement
  ```

- `src/FileManager.Service/Program.cs:75`

  ```csharp
  // The process-wide scan scheduler owns all directory-enumeration worker threads (global +
  // per-drive budgets), shared by the source scan and the destination sweep.
  services.AddSingleton<IScanScheduler, ScanScheduler>();
  ```


**Why it matters.** This is the component that decides how many OS threads the service pins against the user's disks. The failure modes are both user-visible and both unguarded today: a decrement that runs twice (there are three separate `_liveWorkers--` sites, one in a catch block at line 128) permanently under-counts and the pool starves — dry runs and jobs stall with no error; a decrement that is missed lets the pool grow past MaxScanThreads and thrash the disk. Neither is a compile error and neither is observable from outside the class, so any refactor of the claim/park/re-arm machinery in this 692-LOC file is unverifiable.

**Proposed change.** In src/FileManager.Core/Scanning/ScanScheduler.cs make two minimal changes (FileManager.Core already grants InternalsVisibleTo to FileManager.Core.Tests at FileManager.Core.csproj:26, so no csproj edit is needed):

1. Replace the const at line 32 with an instance field and an internal setter used only by tests:
   private int _idleTimeoutMs = 15_000;
   internal int IdleTimeoutMs { get => _idleTimeoutMs; set => _idleTimeoutMs = value; }
   and use `_idleTimeoutMs` at line 114.

2. Add an internal observer next to the field at line 43:
   internal int LiveWorkers { get { lock (_lock) { return _liveWorkers; } } }

Then extend tests/FileManager.Core.Tests/Scanning/ScanSchedulerTests.cs with four facts driven by the existing FakeSettingsProvider (tests/FileManager.Core.Tests/TestSupport/Fakes.cs:116) and the fake file system already used there:
   - Global_cap_bounds_live_workers: set ScanThreading.MaxScanThreads to 2, submit work on four distinct volume keys, assert LiveWorkers never exceeds 2 while work is in flight.
   - Workers_ramp_up_to_the_cap_as_work_arrives: assert LiveWorkers grows from 0 to the cap across successive submits, not to more.
   - Idle_workers_retire: set IdleTimeoutMs = 50, drain all work, poll until LiveWorkers == 0 within a 5s deadline.
   - A_retired_pool_respawns_for_new_work: after the above, submit a new root and assert it completes and LiveWorkers returns above 0.
   - Worker_count_returns_to_zero_after_shutdown: assert LiveWorkers == 0 after disposal, covering the `if (_shutdown)` decrement path at line 107.

**Blast radius.** 2 files, 0 call sites.

IdleTimeoutMs and _liveWorkers have no references outside ScanScheduler.cs (grep across src/, tests/, benchmarks/ returns only the six lines inside this file). ScanScheduler is registered once (Program.cs:75) and constructed directly in 7 test files, none of which pass these members. Purely additive to the type's surface; no behavior change when the setter is not used.

**Verification.** Run tests/FileManager.Core.Tests/Scanning plus the suites that drive the scheduler indirectly (DryRun/DryRunEngineTests, DryRun/DestinationProjectorTests, Watching/SourceScannerTests) — those exercise the same worker pool and would surface an accidental change to the wait semantics. The production default (15_000) is unchanged, so no runtime behavior moves.

**Verifier note.** Evidence verified line for line: private const IdleTimeoutMs = 15_000 (:32), private int _liveWorkers (:43), three decrement sites (:107, :116, :128), and the five existing facts in ScanSchedulerTests.cs observe none of it. Core already grants InternalsVisibleTo to Core.Tests, so the production change really is two lines with no default-behavior movement. Making the process-wide OS-thread ceiling observable on the component that decides disk pressure is legitimate sprint work. Downgraded from high because no defect exists — the double-decrement and missed-decrement modes are hypothetical (I traced WorkerLoop: the two early returns exit outside the try's catch, so the catch at :128 is only reached from Process, no double-decrement today). Prerequisite: of the five proposed facts, the ramp-up and the poll-until-zero retirement tests are wall-clock-timing assertions and are the flaky kind; write them with generous deadlines or drop them, and keep the two that are deterministic (cap never exceeded while work is in flight; LiveWorkers == 0 after Dispose). Trading five test-timing flakes for one observability seam would be a bad deal.

**Why it matters.** The two row types must expose byte-identical member names because the same two flyout templates in DryRunView.axaml bind them with compiled bindings disabled — a rename on one side produces a dead menu item, not a build error. Today nothing enforces that, and the code-behind pays for it with two type-switches (DryRunView.axaml.cs:67 and :161) that exist purely to reach the same-named property on two unrelated types. **Proposed change.** 1. Add to src/FileManager.UI/ViewModels/DryRunViewModel.cs:

```csharp
/// <summary>The row-level file menu contract. Both flat-list row types implement it so the shared
/// x:CompileBindings="False" flyout templates in DryRunView.axaml bind the same member names on
/// either type — the compiler now enforces what the markup assumes.</summary>
public interface IDryRunFileMenuRow
{
    IRelayCommand CopyPathCommand { get; }
    IRelayCommand CopyNameCommand { get; }
    IRelayCommand CopyNameWithoutExtensionCommand { get; }
    IRelayCommand OpenFileCommand { get; }
    IRelayCommand RevealInExplorerCommand { get; }
}

internal static class DryRunRowCommands
{
    public static IRelayCommand CopyPath(IDryRunItemActions? a, Func<string> path) => new RelayCommand(() => a?.CopyText(path()));
    public static IRelayCommand CopyName(IDryRunItemActions? a, Func<string> name) => new RelayCommand(() => a?.CopyText(name()));
    public static IRelayCommand CopyStem(IDryRunItemActions? a, Func<string> name) =>
        new RelayCommand(() => a?.CopyText(Path.GetFileNameWithoutExtension(name())),
                         () => Path.GetFileNameWithoutExtension(name()).Length > 0);
    public static IRelayCommand OpenFile(IDryRunItemActions? a, Func<string> path) =>
        new RelayCommand(() => a?.OpenFile(path()), () => File.Exists(path()));
    public static IRelayCommand Reveal(IDryRunItemActions? a, Func<string> path) =>
        new RelayCommand(() => a?.RevealInExplorer(path()), () => File.Exists(path()));
}
```

2. Declare `public sealed partial record DryRunFileRow(...) : IDryRunFileMenuRow` and `public sealed partial record DryRunDestinationRow(...) : IDryRunFileMenuRow`, and rewrite each of the ten command properties as a one-line delegation, e.g. on DryRunFileRow `public IRelayCommand CopyPathCommand => DryRunRowCommands.CopyPath(Actions, () => SourcePath);` and on DryRunDestinationRow `public IRelayCommand CopyPathCommand => DryRunRowCommands.CopyPath(Actions, () => Primary.TargetPath);`. Keep them as get-only expression-bodied properties declared ON the concrete records — do NOT use default interface members: the flyouts bind by reflection on the runtime type, and DIMs are not visible there.
3. Collapse DryRunView.axaml.cs:161-172 to `if (item is not IDryRunFileMenuRow r) return;` followed by direct use of `r.CopyPathCommand` etc., and DryRunView.axaml.cs:65-70 to `ICommand? open = (dataContext as IDryRunFileMenuRow)?.OpenFileCommand;`.

**Blast radius.** 2 files, 12 call sites.

10 command property declarations in DryRunViewModel.cs (:66-77, :266-276) plus 2 type-switches in DryRunView.axaml.cs (:65-70, :161-172). The four x:CompileBindings="False" regions in DryRunView.axaml (lines 62, 111, 506, 644) are unchanged — every bound member name is preserved.

**Verification.** tests/FileManager.UI.Tests/DryRunViewSmokeTests.cs loads DryRunView headlessly. Add a unit test that, for one DryRunFileRow and one DryRunDestinationRow, asserts CopyNameWithoutExtensionCommand.CanExecute(null) is false for a name of ".git" and true for "a.txt", and that each command property returns a NEW instance per get (the record-equality invariant documented at DryRunViewModel.cs:58-63). Manually exercise both right-click flyouts once, since their bindings are reflection-resolved.

**Verifier note.** Evidence holds: DryRunViewModel.cs:66-77 and :266-276 declare the same five command names with the same empty-stem and File.Exists rules, and DryRunView.axaml.cs carries two type-switches (the switch expression near :67 and the switch statement near :161) that exist only to reach identically-named members on two unrelated types.
