The IDryRunFileMenuRow interface is genuinely valuable — it converts a runtime-only, x:CompileBindings="False" naming contract into a compile-time one and collapses both type-switches. The DryRunRowCommands static helper is not: it replaces ten short, heavily-commented expression-bodied properties with ten one-liners that each allocate a Func<string> closure, and the existing comments at :59-65 and :262-265 already document the per-get / value-equality invariant that the helper would push out of sight. - `tests/FileManager.Core.Tests/DryRun/DryRunEngineTests.cs:667`



**Why it matters.** Every change to dry-run semantics — a new OperationKind, a conflict-resolution rule, a filter behavior — has to be made and re-tested in two pipelines, and only one of them ships. The evidence is in the test suite: DryRunEngineTests and DryRunPipelineTests together call SimulateAsync 12 times to assert report shape, policy outcomes, truncation, faults and cancellation, and DryRunEngineTests.cs:658 exists purely to compare the two pipelines' truncation behavior against each other. That is maintenance paid on a path the product never executes, plus ~250 LOC of Core (ReportBuilder, MaxReportBytes/MaxReportedFiles/ReportByteBudget/MaxBatchCandidates, SimulateAsync) carried in the 1150-line file that is already the largest engine class.

**Proposed change.** Two-step, in this order. (1) Port coverage: for each of the 12 SimulateAsync call sites in tests/FileManager.Core.Tests/DryRun/DryRunEngineTests.cs (:137, :273, :315, :456, :487, :606, :667) and DryRunPipelineTests.cs (:55, :107, :129, :168, :194, :284), rewrite the assertion against SimulateStreamAsync using the existing CollectStream helper in DryRunEngineTests; drop the two that assert only batched-specific byte-budget truncation (DryRunEngineTests.cs:273, :315) since MaxReportBytes disappears with the path. (2) Delete: DryRunEngine.SimulateAsync (:123-241), the nested ReportBuilder (:642-758), the constants MaxReportBytes (:57), MaxReportedFiles (:58) and the seams ReportByteBudget (:83), MaxBatchCandidates (:95); the SimulateAsync member from IDryRunEngine (:15); src/FileManager.Core/IPC/Handlers/DryRunHandler.cs entirely and its two Program.cs registrations; tests/FileManager.Core.Tests/IPC/Handlers/DryRunHandlerTests.cs; the SimulateAsync stub from the three fake engines in DryRunStreamHandlerTests.cs (:31, :163, :362); the DryRunRequest round-trip at tests/FileManager.Service.Tests/EndToEndSmokeTests.cs:187-188 (replace with the streamed request it already exercises); and benchmarks/FileManager.Core.Benchmarks/DryRun/DryRunEngineBenchmarks.cs:169 (retarget to SimulateStreamAsync).

Migration story for the frozen wire surface: do NOT touch Contracts. DryRunRequest, DryRunResponse and their "dry-run"/"dry-run-report" discriminators, IpcRequestTypes.DryRun and its DiscriminatorOf case, and the SerializationTests that pin them all stay exactly as they are — the wire vocabulary is unchanged and IpcRequestTypesTests still passes. Removing only the handler means the discriminator drops out of the dispatch dictionary and a sender would get NOT_IMPLEMENTED; since no protocol-6 client sends it (verified above), also bump IpcRequest.CurrentProtocolVersion 6 → 7 so any pre-streaming build fails loud with IPC_VERSION_MISMATCH instead, and record the removal in docs/specs/architecture-v1.md §8.

**Blast radius.** 11 files, 14 call sites.

src (5): DryRunEngine.cs, IDryRunEngine.cs, DryRunHandler.cs (delete), Program.cs (2 registration lines), IpcRequest.cs (version bump only). tests (5): DryRunEngineTests.cs (7 calls), DryRunPipelineTests.cs (6 calls), DryRunHandlerTests.cs (delete), DryRunStreamHandlerTests.cs (3 stubs), EndToEndSmokeTests.cs (1). benchmarks (1): DryRunEngineBenchmarks.cs. Contracts records and their SerializationTests are deliberately untouched.

**Verification.** Before deleting anything, land step (1) alone and confirm the ported tests pass against SimulateStreamAsync — that proves the streamed path covers what the batched tests asserted. Then run the whole suite: tests/FileManager.Core.Tests/IPC/IpcRequestTypesTests.cs and tests/FileManager.Contracts.Tests/IPC/SerializationTests.cs must still pass untouched (proving the wire vocabulary did not move), and tests/FileManager.Service.Tests/EndToEndSmokeTests.cs must still complete its dry run over the real pipe.

**Verifier note.** The factual core holds: SimulateAsync's only production caller is DryRunHandler.cs:30, and no UI code references DryRunRequest/DryRunResponse/SimulateAsync (verified by repo-wide grep). But the remedy is a product decision wearing a refactor's clothes, and its blast radius is out of proportion to ~250 LOC. It deletes a live IPC handler, rewrites 12 tests on the safety-critical deletion-preview engine, drops the MaxReportBytes 16 MiB frame-cap machinery, and — per its own migration story — bumps IpcRequest.CurrentProtocolVersion 6→7, a frozen cross-process surface where the service may already be running from an older build. The engine's own doc comment at DryRunEngine.cs:34 designates SimulateAsync as the batched/CLI path, and docs/specs/architecture-v1.md:184 lists FileManager.Cli.exe as a planned component (its §2.2 command table at :1236 does not yet include dry-run, which is why this survives at all rather than being killed outright). PREREQUISITE: a human decision that the batched/CLI dry-run is abandoned and that a protocol bump is wanted, recorded in the spec. Do not let an agent execute this unilaterally. Note it also conflicts with the phase-3 finding — deleting the batched path resolves that duplication for free, so these two must not both be actioned.

#### `runprofile-detached-scan-escapes-host-lifetime` — RunProfileHandler launches an unowned background scan that no layer can observe, cancel, or drain at shutdown

| | |
|---|---|
| Lens | layering-dependencies |
| Severity | low (verifier verdict: downgrade) |
| Confidence | high |
| Effort | small |
| Risk flags | changes-behavior, no-test-coverage |

**Claim.** A folder-scoped manual run fires `Task.Run(..., CancellationToken.None)` from inside the IPC handler. The resulting enumeration is owned by nothing: EngineHost's shutdown sequence drains only the orchestrator, so the scan keeps enqueuing into a queue whose consumer has stopped, and publishes its terminal RunQueuedEvent after the event bridge to IPC subscribers has been disposed.

**Evidence.**

- `src/FileManager.Core/IPC/Handlers/RunProfileHandler.cs:85`

  ```csharp
  _ = Task.Run(() => ScanAndEnqueue(profile, typed.Path, runId), CancellationToken.None);
  ```

- `src/FileManager.Service/EngineHost.cs:164`

  ```csharp
  await orchestrator.StopAsync();
  _profilesBridge?.Dispose();
  _pauseBridge?.Dispose();
  _eventBridge?.Dispose();
  await ipcServer.StopAsync(CancellationToken.None);
  ```

- `src/FileManager.Core/Jobs/JobOrchestrator.cs:68`

  ```csharp
  await _consumer.ConfigureAwait(false);                       // stop dequeuing
  await Task.WhenAll(_running.Keys).ConfigureAwait(false);     // drain in-flight (I-ATOMIC-JOB)
  ```

- `src/FileManager.Core/IPC/Handlers/RunProfileHandler.cs:129`

  ```csharp
  // Always terminate the run, even on a fault or a zero-match scan: this event is the ONLY way
  // a caller that got Scanning=true learns the outcome.
  ```


**Why it matters.** The handler's own comment says the RunQueuedEvent is the only way a client that received Scanning=true learns the outcome. If the user closes the app (which, in StartAndStopWithProgram mode, calls ShutdownServiceAsync) while a large folder scan is running, the enqueued payloads are dropped by a stopped consumer and the completion event fires into a disposed bridge — the UI shows neither "queued N files" nor an error, and the run silently never happened. The scan also holds ScanScheduler LongRunning worker threads that nothing waits on. No component in the composition root can see this work exists.

**Proposed change.** Give the background enumeration an owner with a lifetime. Minimal version: inject `IHostApplicationLifetime`-equivalent cancellation into RunProfileHandler by adding a `CancellationToken` source the host controls — concretely, add a small `IBackgroundWorkTracker` to src/FileManager.Core/Observability/ with `void Track(Func<CancellationToken, Task> work)` and `Task DrainAsync()`, backed by a ConcurrentDictionary<Task,byte> and a linked CancellationTokenSource (mirror JobOrchestrator.cs:33/60-70, which already implements exactly this pattern). Register it in src/FileManager.Service/Program.cs beside the other Core singletons, inject it into RunProfileHandler in place of the bare `Task.Run` at line 85, and await `DrainAsync()` in EngineHost.RunAsync between `await orchestrator.StopAsync();` (EngineHost.cs:164) and `_eventBridge?.Dispose();` (line 167) so the terminal RunQueuedEvent still reaches subscribers. Pass the tracker's token into `scanner.Scan(profile, TriggerKind.ManualShell, folder, ct)` at RunProfileHandler.cs:103 so a shutdown cuts the walk short and the handler publishes RunQueuedEvent with the partial count plus an Error, which is already the shape ScanAndEnqueue produces on a fatal fault.

**Blast radius.** 4 files, 1 call site.

One Task.Run site (RunProfileHandler.cs:85). Touches RunProfileHandler.cs, a new Core file, Program.cs (1 registration + no other handler changes), EngineHost.cs (1 await). RunProfileHandler is constructed at 1 DI site (Program.cs:121) and 1 test site (EndToEndSmokeTests.cs:110) — both constructor signatures gain one parameter. tests/FileManager.Core.Tests/IPC/Handlers/Set3HandlersTests.cs also constructs it.

**Verification.** Add a Core test: start a folder run against a source tree, call DrainAsync concurrently, and assert exactly one RunQueuedEvent is observed on the bus and that no payload is enqueued after the drain returns. Existing coverage: tests/FileManager.Core.Tests/IPC/Handlers/Set3HandlersTests.cs already exercises RunProfileHandler's file and folder branches; those must stay green.

**Verifier note.** The mechanism is real — RunProfileHandler.cs:85 fires `Task.Run(..., CancellationToken.None)` and calls scanner.Scan with no token, EngineHost.cs:164-168 drains only the orchestrator and then disposes the event bridge. But the harm is overstated, because TriggerQueue is a purely in-memory LinkedList (src/FileManager.Core/Watching/TriggerQueue.cs) with no persistence: EVERY pending payload is dropped at shutdown by design, so 'the scan keeps enqueuing into a stopped consumer' is not a defect specific to this call site. What is left is a shutdown-only edge case where a walk keeps burning scan-scheduler threads while the process is trying to exit, and one terminal event fires into a disposed bridge — at a moment when the UI that would consume it is closing. Downgraded to low, and the proposed remedy is oversized for it: a new IBackgroundWorkTracker abstraction in Core/Observability, a DI registration, and a change to the shutdown ordering (an area governed by I-ATOMIC-JOB) for a single call site is speculative generality. If this is done, do the minimal version only: thread the host's stopping CancellationToken into RunProfileHandler and pass it to scanner.Scan at :103 so the walk stops promptly; skip the tracker.

17 AddSingleton lines + 17 GetRequiredService lines, all inside src/FileManager.Service/Program.cs:119-162. No consumer outside that file resolves a concrete handler type.

**Verification.** tests/FileManager.Service.Tests/EndToEndSmokeTests.cs drives 14 request types through a real named pipe; if any handler dropped out of the table it fails with NOT_IMPLEMENTED. Additionally assert the resolved dictionary has 17 entries and that its key set equals IpcRequestTypes' const table — that check does not exist today and would close the gap permanently.

**Verifier note.** Verified exactly: Program.cs:119-135 registers 17 concrete handlers, :138-157 re-lists the same 17 via GetRequiredService, :158-161 folds them into the table. I also verified the precondition the finding asserts — all 17 GetRequiredService<*Handler> occurrences in src/ are inside that factory, so nothing else resolves a concrete handler type. The change removes one of the three hand-maintained parallel tables the constraints register flags as unguarded ("Nothing pins the DI list"), keeps registration fully explicit (no assembly scanning, AOT rule preserved), and is one file. Duplicate-RequestType behavior is unchanged (ToDictionary throws at first resolution just as table.Add does today). Cheap, safe, permanently closes a silent NOT_IMPLEMENTED failure mode. Do include the suggested assertion that the resolved key set equals IpcRequestTypes' const table.

#### `batched-dryrun-sweep-unbounded` — The destination-sweep memory bound added for the streamed dry run was never applied to the batched dry run

| | |
|---|---|
| Lens | divergent-parallel-modules |
| Severity | low (verifier verdict: downgrade) |
| Confidence | high |
| Effort | trivial |
| Risk flags | changes-behavior, perf-sensitive |

**Claim.** DestinationProjector.Sweep takes a maxEntries budget that defaults to int.MaxValue. DryRunStreamHandler passes a real budget derived from the file cap, with a comment explaining that without it "a target root with millions of pre-existing files can't buffer an unbounded op-per-file set service-side". DryRunEngine.SimulateAsync — the batched half of the same feature, reachable over the wire as DryRunRequest — calls the same method and omits the argument, so it materializes the full sweep result in memory before the byte budget trims it.

**Evidence.**

- `src/FileManager.Core/DryRun/DestinationProjector.cs:72`

  ```csharp
  public DestinationSweepResult Sweep(
      Profile profile, ISet<NormalizedPath> survivors, bool truncated, CancellationToken ct,
      int maxEntries = int.MaxValue, DryRunProgressCounters? progress = null)
  ```

- `src/FileManager.Core/IPC/Handlers/DryRunStreamHandler.cs:181`

  ```csharp
  // Bound the sweep by the same overall file budget the source phase uses, so a target root
  // with millions of pre-existing files can't buffer an unbounded op-per-file set service-side.
  int sweepBudget = Math.Max(0, MaxStreamedFiles - destinationCount);
  ```

- `src/FileManager.Core/DryRun/DryRunEngine.cs:204`

  ```csharp
  DestinationSweepResult sweep = scanDestinations
      ? destinationProjector.Sweep(profile, builder.Survivors, truncated, ct)
      : new DestinationSweepResult([], []);
  ```

- `src/FileManager.Core/DryRun/DryRunEngine.cs:207`

  ```csharp
  for (int i = 0; i < sweep.Files.Count; i++)
  {
      if (!builder.TryAddSweepEntry(sweep.Files[i], sweep.Ops[i]))   // byte budget applied only AFTER the full sweep is materialized
  ```


**Why it matters.** The batched path's ReportByteBudget bounds the *report*, not the sweep: by the time TryAddSweepEntry starts rejecting entries, DestinationProjector has already built one PhysicalFile plus one VirtualFileOperation for every pre-existing file under every target root, on the service process's heap. A DryRunRequest against a profile whose target is a large existing archive can therefore exhaust service memory — the exact failure the streamed path was hardened against. Both halves of one feature call the same collaborator; the hardening landed on one of them. The same asymmetry holds for progress counters (streamed only) and the space projection (streamed only), which is the standing cost of maintaining two pipelines for one capability: the batched half has no client in src/FileManager.UI (a repo-wide grep for DryRunRequest finds only Contracts, Core, tests and benchmarks) so its divergence goes unnoticed.

**Proposed change.** In src/FileManager.Core/DryRun/DryRunEngine.cs, mirror the streamed handler's bound at the SimulateAsync sweep call (line 204-206):

    int sweepBudget = Math.Max(0, MaxBatchCandidates - builder.DestinationFiles.Count);
    DestinationSweepResult sweep = scanDestinations
        ? destinationProjector.Sweep(profile, builder.Survivors, truncated, ct, sweepBudget)
        : new DestinationSweepResult([], []);

and set `truncated = true` when `sweep.Truncated` is set, matching DryRunStreamHandler.cs:216-222, so a capped sweep is reported to the caller rather than silently short. MaxBatchCandidates already exists as the batched path's file cap (DryRunEngine.cs:95) and is already used as the scan cap at line 155.

Separately (not part of this change, but the reason the bug existed): DryRunHandler + IDryRunEngine.SimulateAsync + ReportBuilder are a second implementation of a capability whose only production client uses DryRunStreamRequest. Retiring them would require deleting the frozen wire records DryRunRequest/DryRunResponse and bumping IpcRequest.CurrentProtocolVersion from 6 to 7 — a valid migration because a version mismatch already fails loud with IPC_VERSION_MISMATCH (src/FileManager.Core/IPC/IpcServer.cs:238-243) — plus updating ~12 SimulateAsync call sites in tests/FileManager.Core.Tests/DryRun and one in benchmarks/FileManager.Core.Benchmarks/DryRun/DryRunEngineBenchmarks.cs:169. Raise that as its own decision; do not fold it into the budget fix.

**Blast radius.** 1 file, 2 call sites.

The budget fix touches only src/FileManager.Core/DryRun/DryRunEngine.cs:204-218. DestinationProjector.Sweep has 3 call sites total: DryRunEngine.cs:205, DryRunStreamHandler.cs:192, and DestinationProjector.Project (DestinationProjector.cs:56, used by unit tests) — the last also defaults maxEntries and is test-only, so leave it. The optional retirement of the batched path would touch ~6 source files, 4 test files and 1 benchmark.

**Verification.** Run tests/FileManager.Core.Tests/DryRun/DestinationProjectorTests.cs (it already covers the maxEntries cap and the Truncated flag) and DryRunEngineTests.cs / DryRunPipelineTests.cs, which pin the batched report's truncation semantics and referential integrity — the new sweep cap must not break the invariant that no retained operation references a dropped file. Add one test that gives a batched profile more pre-existing destination files than MaxBatchCandidates (shrink the seam) and asserts Report.Truncated is true.

**Verifier note.** Evidence exact: DestinationProjector.Sweep defaults maxEntries to int.MaxValue, DryRunStreamHandler.cs:178-181 passes a real budget with the explaining comment, and DryRunEngine.cs:204-206 omits it while :207-218 applies the byte budget only after the full sweep is materialized. Genuine divergence between two halves of one feature, and the fix is three lines using MaxBatchCandidates, which already exists as the batched cap. Downgraded to low because the finding's own research shows the exhaustion is unreachable in production — no UI client ever sends DryRunRequest, so the batched path is exercised only by tests, EndToEndSmokeTests and the wire contract. Fix it because it costs nothing and restores parity, not because a user can hit it. EXPLICITLY EXCLUDE the rider: do NOT retire DryRunHandler/DryRunRequest/DryRunResponse or bump IpcRequest.CurrentProtocolVersion to 7 — those are frozen wire records and that is a separate decision the finding itself says not to fold in.

#### `corrupt-settings-file-silently-replaced-by-defaults` — An unparseable settings.json falls back to defaults and the first later save overwrites it, destroying the user's stored configuration with no copy kept

| | |
|---|---|
| Lens | error-handling-failure-modes |
| Severity | low (verifier verdict: downgrade) |
| Confidence | high |
| Effort | trivial |
| Risk flags | changes-behavior, no-test-coverage |

**Claim.** SettingsService.Load catches JsonException/IOException, logs a warning and returns GlobalSettings.Default. The unreadable file is left in place and the next Update writes over it, so the original bytes — including the user's relocated ProfilesDirectory — are gone permanently.

**Evidence.**

- `src/FileManager.Core/Settings/SettingsService.cs:97`

  ```csharp
  catch (Exception ex) when (ex is JsonException or IOException or UnauthorizedAccessException)
  {
      _logger.LogWarning(ex, "Settings file {File} could not be loaded; using defaults", file);
      return GlobalSettings.Default;
  }
  ```

- `src/FileManager.Core/Settings/SettingsService.cs:58`

  ```csharp
  File.Move(tempPath, finalPath, overwrite: true);
  ```

- `src/FileManager.Core/Profiles/ProfileStore.cs:25`

  ```csharp
  private string ProfilesDirectory => settings.Current.ProfilesDirectory;
  ```


**Why it matters.** settings.json holds the relocated ProfilesDirectory, and ProfileStore resolves that live on every read. A file that cannot be parsed — a partial write from an older build, an interrupted external edit, disk-level corruption — therefore does not merely reset the theme: it points the engine at the default profiles folder, so the user's entire profile set disappears from the UI (see the empty-catalog finding for what that looks like), and the first settings save from the UI rewrites the file, making the original path unrecoverable. Recovery today requires the user to remember where they had moved the folder.

**Proposed change.** In src/FileManager.Core/Settings/SettingsService.Load, before returning GlobalSettings.Default from either catch (lines 97-107) and from the deserialized-to-null branch at line 90, preserve the original: wrap in its own try/catch and `File.Move(file, file + ".corrupt-" + DateTime.UtcNow.ToString("yyyyMMddHHmmss"), overwrite: false)`, logging at Error (not Warning) with both paths. This makes the subsequent Update a fresh write rather than a destructive overwrite and leaves the user's configuration recoverable by hand. Keep the fallback-to-defaults behaviour itself — refusing to start the service on a bad settings file is worse.

**Blast radius.** 1 file, 3 call sites.

SettingsService.cs only; three return-defaults sites inside the private Load method, which is called exactly once from the constructor (line 39).

**Verification.** Add a test alongside the existing SettingsService suite in tests/FileManager.Core.Tests/Disposition/SourceDispositionServiceTests.cs's sibling settings section: write `{ garbage` to <root>/settings.json, construct SettingsService, assert Current equals GlobalSettings.Default AND that a settings.json.corrupt-* file now exists while settings.json does not. Then call Update and assert the corrupt copy survives.

**Verifier note.** Code is as cited (SettingsService.cs:90-94 and :97-107 return GlobalSettings.Default and leave the file in place; :53-58 makes the next Update a temp+fsync+rename overwrite). The consequence chain — losing a relocated ProfilesDirectory permanently — is correctly reasoned. Downgraded to low on probability: settings.json is written atomically with an fsync before the rename, so partial writes are largely designed out, and a newer-schema file deserializes rather than throwing; the realistic triggers are hand-editing and disk-level corruption. The fix is ~6 defensive lines with no behavior change on the happy path, which is why it survives at all. Two corrections for whoever executes it: the proposed test location is wrong (SourceDispositionServiceTests is unrelated — the settings suite is tests/FileManager.Core.Tests/Settings/SettingsServiceTests.cs), and the rename must itself be wrapped so a failure to quarantine still falls back to defaults rather than faulting service startup.

#### `storagebar-band-layout-inside-render` — StorageBar's band geometry and threshold colouring are computed inside Render(DrawingContext) and cannot be tested

**Claim.** All of StorageBar's decision logic — which bands exist, their extents, the net-frees inversion when settled < used, the over-margin red/amber escalation, and the left-to-right band ordering that drives hover hit-testing — lives inside `Render(DrawingContext)`, interleaved with `context.DrawRectangle` calls. It is reachable only through a real render pass. The one smoke test that touches the control (DryRunViewSmokeTests.Storage_panel_and_bars_lay_out_with_a_projection) asserts layout, not band values.

**Evidence.**

- `src/FileManager.UI/Controls/StorageBar.cs:166`

  ```csharp
  bool overRed = RealisticPeakBytes > marginLine;
  bool overAmber = SafeCeilingBytes > marginLine;
  ```

- `src/FileManager.UI/Controls/StorageBar.cs:171`

  ```csharp
  {
      Seg(0, used, usedNow, "CSU", "Current Storage Used", LabelLight);

  else
  {
  ```

- `src/FileManager.UI/Controls/PathTruncation.cs:24`

  ```csharp
  /// <summary>Character-count based path shortening. Kept UI-free (no Avalonia types) so the branching
  ```
