
- `src/FileManager.UI/ViewModels/DryRunViewModel.cs:2169`

  ```csharp
  // Warnings mirror the bar: red once the realistic peak crosses capacity − margin (likely
  // won't fit / very tight), amber once only the safe ceiling does (worst case gets close).
  long marginLine = v.TotalCapacityBytes - marginBytes;
  ```

- `tests/FileManager.UI.Tests/DryRunViewModelTests.cs:1307`

  ```csharp
  public async Task Space_projection_populates_volume_rows_with_state_driven_warnings()
  ```


**Why it matters.** The threshold rule is deliberately written twice — VolumeSpaceRow's warning text (DryRunViewModel.cs:2169, tested) and StorageBar's colouring (StorageBar.cs:166, untested) — with the comment "Warnings mirror the bar" as the only link. The bar is what a user reads before committing a run that may fill a drive; if the two drift, the row says "the peak usage may exceed the free space" while the bar stays calm blue, or vice versa. The repo already established the fix pattern in the same folder: PathText's rules were split into the UI-free PathTruncation precisely so they could be unit-tested, and PathTruncationTests exists.

**Proposed change.** Follow the PathTruncation precedent in src/FileManager.UI/Controls/.

1. New file src/FileManager.UI/Controls/StorageBandLayout.cs, no Avalonia types:
   internal enum StorageBandRole { UsedNow, AddedAtRest, Freed, Transient, WorstCase }
   internal readonly record struct StorageBand(double FromBytes, double ToBytes, StorageBandRole Role, string Acronym, string Expanded, bool OverRed, bool OverAmber);
   internal static class StorageBandLayout {
       public static IReadOnlyList<StorageBand> Compute(double capacityBytes, double usedNowBytes, double settledBytes, double realisticPeakBytes, double safeCeilingBytes, double marginBytes);
       public static double? MarginLineBytes(double capacityBytes, double marginBytes);   // null when the line falls outside (0, capacity)
   }
   Move lines 160-194 of StorageBar.cs into Compute verbatim: the peak/ceiling Math.Max clamping, overRed/overAmber, the settled>=used branch, and the two trailing Seg calls — emitting StorageBand values instead of drawing. Compute returns bands in the same emission order (the hit-test scans newest-first, so order is behavior).

2. Render becomes: `foreach (StorageBand b in StorageBandLayout.Compute(...))` → map Role+OverRed/OverAmber to the brush (the existing Band(...) palette lookup and the LabelLight/LabelDark choice stay in the control), clamp/scale to pixels, DrawRectangle, append to _bands, DrawLabel. MarginLineBytes replaces the inline `if (marginLine > 0 && marginLine < cap)` guard at line 190.

3. Add tests/FileManager.UI.Tests/StorageBandLayoutTests.cs covering: growth case (settled > used) emits CSU then SUAR then RPSU then APSU in that order; net-frees case (settled < used) emits SUAR then a Freed band and no CSU; zero-width bands (settled == used) are omitted; OverRed is set exactly when realisticPeak > capacity - margin and OverAmber exactly when safeCeiling > capacity - margin (add the boundary case where they are equal); a band whose To exceeds capacity is clamped; MarginLineBytes returns null when margin >= capacity or margin == 0. Add one cross-check test asserting Compute's OverRed/OverAmber agree with VolumeSpaceRow.IsDanger/IsWarning for the same inputs, so the two copies of the rule can no longer drift silently.

**Blast radius.** 2 files, 1 call site.

StorageBar is instantiated in exactly one place, src/FileManager.UI/Views/DryRunView.axaml:164. Its six styled properties are unchanged, so the XAML and the DryRunSpaceViewModel bindings are untouched. StorageBar is a type-independent control (no ControlTheme keyed by {x:Type}), so no theme coupling is at risk.

**Verification.** Run tests/FileManager.UI.Tests including DryRunViewSmokeTests.Storage_panel_and_bars_lay_out_with_a_projection (headless render must still succeed). Then run the app, open a dry run against a nearly-full drive, and compare the bar colours to the warning text on the same row — they must agree, which is exactly what the new cross-check test asserts.

**Verifier note.** Accurate: StorageBar.cs:160-194 computes clamping, overRed/overAmber, the settled-vs-used inversion, band order and the margin-line guard inline between DrawRectangle calls, and the in-repo precedent is real (PathTruncation.cs:24 with its 'Kept UI-free … so the branching is exercised by plain unit tests' comment, and PathTruncationTests.cs exists). The threshold rule genuinely is written twice (DryRunViewModel.cs:2169 'Warnings mirror the bar'). Downgraded to low: no drift has actually occurred, the control is purely visual, and the extraction moves ordering-sensitive logic (band emission order drives hover hit-testing) for a benefit that is entirely prospective test coverage. If it is picked up, the only part carrying real value is the cross-check test asserting Compute's OverRed/OverAmber agree with VolumeSpaceRow.IsDanger/IsWarning for the same inputs — the geometry extraction is the vehicle for that, not the goal. Not ahead of the staged-replace or handler-table items in any sprint.

## Considered and rejected

11 candidate findings were killed by the churn critic. They are recorded so a later
review does not re-raise them, and as evidence that the filter ran.

#### `dryrun-treenode-model-builder-and-grid-columns` — DryRunTreeNode is six classes in one: node model, forest builder, expansion snapshotter, right-click menu, TreeDataGrid column definitions, and grid row-walker

*Lens:* god-components-srp · *claimed severity:* high

**Claim.** DryRunTreeNode (DryRunViewModel.cs:351-999, ~650 lines) simultaneously (1) models a path-forest node (Name/FullPath/Depth/Children/lazy _leafFactory/SizeBytes/Pills), (2) is its own builder via the static generic BuildForest<T>/BuildLeaves<T>/FinishRecursive/BuildPills/SortRecursive, (3) snapshots and restores expansion state (ApplyExpanded/CollectExpanded), (4) hosts 11 [RelayCommand] menu actions with disk-existence CanExecute guards, (5) declares the TreeDataGrid's column layout — header names, GridLength widths, MinWidth/MaxWidth pixel values, sort comparers and cell-template resource keys — in the static BuildSource, and (6) walks the control's realized row list (FindRow over HierarchicalRow<T>). Items 5 and 6 are pure view concerns: BuildSource is the only reason this file imports Avalonia.Controls and Avalonia.Controls.Models.TreeDataGrid, and it is the only view model in the project that does so.

**Rejected because.** Citations are accurate (BuildSource does declare column geometry at :800-856, FindRow at :524, BuildForest at :563), but the proposal fails on its own stated benefit and is under-specified. (1) The headline justification — "the Avalonia import is what stops this type's tests running without a headless Application" — is not achieved: the proposal explicitly keeps FindRow and DryRunTreeController on DryRunTreeNode, and both reference HierarchicalTreeDataGridSource/HierarchicalRow, so `using Avalonia.Controls` and `Avalonia.Controls.Models.TreeDataGrid` stay in the file. Only `using Avalonia` (GridLength) leaves. (2) The statics it wants moved touch private state on every line: `dir._leafFactory` (:631), `node._counts` (:688, :886-889, :913, :975), `node._sizeBytes` (:690, :891), `root._children` (:654, :746, :879), `node._hasChildren` (:897), `node.Pills` private setter (:936), plus the private ctor. Extracting them requires widening ~7 private fields to internal on the repo's most allocation-sensitive type — the proposal mentions only an "internal factory for the private constructor". A downstream agent executing this mechanically would strip the encapsulation that keeps the lazy-leaf / counts-release invariants local, which is exactly what commit 507d56c ('Fixed tree view allocations and memory leak') was about. Criterion (e). Note also the ActivityViewModel.cs:20 evidence line quotes an inline comment that does not exist in the file (the real text is a <para> in the ActivityRow doc comment).

#### `dryrun-stream-handler-is-a-pipeline-not-a-handler` — DryRunStreamHandler is a three-phase pipeline orchestrator wearing an IPC handler's interface — 305 lines against a 17-41 line sibling set

*Lens:* god-components-srp · *claimed severity:* high

**Claim.** Every other IIpcRequestHandler in src/FileManager.Core/IPC/Handlers/ is 17-41 lines (GetSettingsHandler 17, GetStatusHandler 17, DryRunHandler 41, SaveProfileHandler 38) and does one thing: cast the request, call one collaborator, map the Result to a response. DryRunStreamHandler is 305 lines and owns seven distinct jobs in one method body: profile resolution, driving the engine's chunk enumerator with a hand-rolled MoveNextAsync/Task.WhenAny progress-polling loop (lines 111-133), folding each chunk into a DryRunSpaceEstimator it constructs and times with its own Stopwatch (84, 150-154), accumulating the survivor set for the sweep (94, 155), hosting the blocking destination sweep on a pool thread with a second identical polling loop (190-213), re-chunking the sweep output and rewriting SubjectIndex offsets (236-247), enforcing a second file cap independent of the engine's, and emitting a four-metric timing telemetry line (253-261). It also carries a nested WireChunkConverter (271-304) that owns the report's global directory-index space.

**Rejected because.** Evidence is accurate (305 lines vs 17/38/41-line siblings; two polling loops at 115-133 and 196-213; nested WireChunkConverter at 271-304; DryRunEngine.cs:204 does run the same phase-3 sequence). Killed on (e) disproportionate and (i) self-defeating proposal: the stated cost — phase-3 sweep orchestration existing in two places — is explicitly NOT fixed by the proposed change, which moves the handler's copy to a new file and leaves DryRunEngine.SimulateAsync's copy where it is. What remains is a pure lift-and-shift of a `yield return`/`await using` streaming state machine whose frame ORDER is a wire contract (register: IpcResponse frame order chunks→progress→complete), plus a NEW DryRunStreamFrame discriminated-union translation layer that adds indirection without removing a line of logic. This is the 5th-highest-churn file in the repo and is perf-sensitive; rewriting every yield through a DU for an SRP line-count argument is exactly the well-intentioned churn this gate exists to stop. If the sweep duplication is the real concern, the finding to write is 'extract the phase-3 sweep sequence shared by DryRunEngine.SimulateAsync:204 and DryRunStreamHandler:190-247' — that is a different, smaller, targeted change.

#### `dryrun-engine-two-assemblers-plus-json-sizer` — DryRunEngine bundles the shared scan pipeline with two independent report assemblers and a JSON serialized-size estimator in 1150 lines

*Lens:* god-components-srp · *claimed severity:* medium

**Claim.** DryRunEngine holds four separable concerns in one file: (1) the genuinely shared fused scan+evaluate pipeline (ScanAndEvaluateAsync:453, EvaluateFileAsync:891, EvaluateTargetAsync:1022) — which both entry points correctly reuse; (2) batched report assembly with byte-budget truncation and index remapping (SimulateAsync:123 plus the nested ReportBuilder:642); (3) streamed chunk assembly with global index tracking and carrier recycling (SimulateStreamAsync:256 plus the nested StreamAccumulator:759); and (4) a self-contained JSON serialized-size estimator (lines 833-889) that builds a 128-entry ASCII escape table from JavaScriptEncoder.Default, four UpperBoundBytes overloads and three structural-byte constants. Concern (4) has no dependency on the engine at all and is already reached from tests as a static (DryRunEngineTests.cs:442). Concerns (2) and (3) never interact.

**Rejected because.** Kill under (a) style/organization and (e) disproportionate. Every citation checks out (UnescapedAscii/BuildUnescapedAscii at DryRunEngine.cs:865-873, ReportBuilder at :642, StreamAccumulator at :759, DryRunEngineTests.cs:442 calling DryRunEngine.StringUpperBound), but nothing is broken and nothing is prevented. The stated harms are 'the file is 1150 lines', 'the test class declares six sections', and '27% of commits touch it' — those are organization complaints, not defects, and the finding itself concedes the SimulateAsync/SimulateStreamAsync split is 'the correct factoring'. Pure code motion across a perf-sensitive AOT file in exchange for smaller files is exactly the week-long-zero-measurable-benefit churn this gate exists to stop. If the file genuinely becomes unnavigable, `partial class` splits cost nothing and need no review finding.

#### `dead-uistatestore-parameterless-overloads` — UiStateStore's parameterless Read/Write overloads have no callers

*Lens:* dead-unreachable-code · *claimed severity:* low

**Claim.** `UiStateStore.Read()` and `UiStateStore.Write(UiState)` — the two overloads that resolve the path from `UiPaths.UiStateFilePath` — are never called. Production (MainWindowViewModel) and the tests both go through the path-taking `Read(string)` / `Write(string, UiState)` overloads. The sibling `StartupTheme.Read()` parameterless overload IS called (App.axaml.cs:31), so this is not a symmetric-API convention that is being kept deliberately.

**Rejected because.** The citation is literally correct — UiStateStore.cs:14 and :39 exist and have no callers. Killed on (a)/(e): the whyItMatters is wrong, so nothing is left but two dead one-liners. It claims 'two places now decide where ui-state.json lives', but MainWindowViewModel.cs:47 resolves `uiStatePath ?? UiPaths.UiStateFilePath` — the exact same constant the deleted overloads would use. There is one source of truth, no drift is possible, and no maintenance is saved. Deleting two convenience overloads that mirror the deliberate StartupTheme.Read() shape is taste with no cost attached.

#### `dead-jobstatemachine-target-half` — The per-target half of JobStateMachine is never driven in production

*Lens:* dead-unreachable-code · *claimed severity:* medium

**Claim.** `JobStateMachine.TransitionTarget`, `JobStateMachine.TargetStates`, the `_targetStates` list, and the entire 14-line `TargetEdges` legality table have zero production call sites. `JobExecutor` calls only `states.Transition(JobState.*)` — 17 times — and its own class doc says per-target state lives on the mutable `TargetProgress` mirror instead. The only callers of the target half are three tests in JobStateMachineTests.cs.

**Rejected because.** The call-site claim is accurate (TransitionTarget/TargetStates appear only in JobStateMachine.cs and three JobStateMachineTests cases), but the finding misreads the doc it builds its argument on: JobStateMachine.cs:10-11 ALREADY states 'per-target placement/rollback work off the mutable TargetProgress mirror', so the class does not claim to enforce what it doesn't. What remains is a 14-line legality table that is a faithful transcription of the architecture spec's §7.1 target state diagram, pinned by three passing tests — kill under (b): it is executable documentation of an external normative spec that the repo references by section number, and deleting a spec transcription plus its tests to remove 25 lines is a net loss of auditability. The stated alternative (wire TransitionTarget into JobExecutor at every TargetProgress mutation) is a behavior change to the job pipeline that would throw InvalidOperationException on any sequence the table gets subtly wrong, with no characterization tests — kill under (g) for that branch. Leaving it as-is is the correct third option the finding dismisses.

#### `dead-result-switch-match-overloads` — Result<T,E>.Switch (both overloads) and the three-way Match have no production callers

*Lens:* dead-unreachable-code · *claimed severity:* low

**Claim.** Of the four combinators on `Result<TValue, TError>`, only the two-argument `Match` is used in shipping code (one call site, FileSystemService.cs:169). `Switch(onSuccess, onError)`, `Switch(onSuccess, onError, onCanceled)`, and `Match(onSuccess, onError, onCanceled)` are called only from tests/FileManager.Contracts.Tests/Primitives/ResultTests.cs. Every other consumer in the repo uses the `TryGetValue`/`TryGetError`/`IsCanceled` three-way branch instead.

**Rejected because.** Evidence holds (verified: only FileSystemService.cs:169 and FileSystemServiceTests.cs:208 call a combinator, both the two-arg Match). Killed under (a) style/taste with no cost attached, and because the change makes the API strictly worse. These are ~40 lines of stable, fully-tested combinators on a core primitive; they cost nothing to carry. The proposal deletes the THREE-way overloads — the cancellation-safe ones — while keeping the two-way ones that throw on Canceled, then rewrites the doc comment at :102-103/:123-124 to remove the pointer to the safer overload. On a type whose three-state contract the finding itself says callers already get wrong, removing the correct way to consume it and deleting the 5 tests that pin the throwing behavior is a net negative.

#### `dryrun-phase3-policy-in-transport-handler` — The streamed dry run's destination-sweep and space-projection phases live in the IPC handler, duplicating and diverging from the engine's own phase 3

*Lens:* layering-dependencies · *claimed severity:* medium

**Claim.** DryRunStreamHandler — a message-handler entry point — owns the destination sweep, the survivor accumulation, the truncation-suppression safety rule and the whole space projection. DryRunEngine.SimulateAsync implements the same phase 3 independently. DestinationProjector is injected into both, and the two implementations already disagree: the batched path produces no SpaceProjection at all.

**Rejected because.** Evidence holds — DryRunStreamHandler.cs:145-262 does own the sweep, survivor accumulation, truncation suppression and space projection, and DryRunEngine.cs:197-218 implements the batched counterpart. But the split is documented and deliberate (DryRunEngine.cs:251: "The destination sweep is left to the handler (which runs it after the file phase)"), and the handler's phase 3 is not separable policy — it is fused with wire concerns on every line: SubjectIndex is offset by the running wire destinationCount (:244), the estimator folds against wire index bases (emitted, destinationCount) (:151-153), WireChunkConverter owns one directory-index space spanning both phases (:95-98, :271-304), and the progress frames are interleaved into the sweep's polling loop (:196-213). Moving phase 3 into the engine means redesigning DryRunChunk to carry terminal state and re-deriving all of that — a rewrite of the streaming producer on a perf-sensitive path whose frame ORDER is a wire contract, for the benefit of stating one safety rule once instead of twice. Criterion (e). If the duplication is the concern, the cheap resolution is the batched-path decision above, not rewriting the shipping pipeline.

#### `relocate-handler-owns-profile-store-file-semantics` — RelocateProfilesHandler re-implements ProfileStore's on-disk naming rule inside the transport layer

*Lens:* layering-dependencies · *claimed severity:* medium

**Claim.** A four-phase copy/commit/delete/reload transaction over the profiles directory lives in an IIpcRequestHandler. It does not take IProfileStore; it reaches straight for Directory.EnumerateFiles/File.Copy/File.Delete and re-derives the "a profile file is a Guid-\"D\"-named *.json" rule that ProfileStore owns.

**Rejected because.** Kill under (c) speculative generality and (e) disproportionate. The code is as described (RelocateProfilesHandler.cs:68-71 filters by Guid parse; ProfileStore.cs:195 owns ProfileFilePath), but the finding is filed as a layering break and there is no layering break — the handler lives in FileManager.Core/IPC/Handlers, the same assembly as ProfileStore, so nothing crosses a boundary. No defect is demonstrated: the handler's Guid filter is strictly more conservative than ProfileStore's deserialize-and-skip and its comment already points at ProfileFilePath as the source of the rule. The stated benefit — 'the only way to re-drive it is to synthesise a request' — is reuse for a repair path and a CLI that do not exist. Against that: widening IProfileStore (a DI-registered Core interface) with a new Result-returning method plus a new RelocationOutcome record, moving a 130-line four-phase transaction with rollback semantics, and re-pointing four existing handler tests, all to relocate working code. Not a sprint item.

#### `streaming-handler-forced-throwing-stub` — IIpcStreamingRequestHandler inherits HandleAsync, so every streaming handler ships an unreachable throwing implementation of the sibling contract

*Lens:* divergent-parallel-modules · *claimed severity:* medium

**Claim.** IIpcStreamingRequestHandler extends IIpcRequestHandler purely to inherit `string RequestType`, which forces every streaming implementation to supply a HandleAsync that throws. Sixteen handlers honour the IIpcRequestHandler contract; the seventeenth throws NotSupportedException from it, and the test double does the same. The dispatch table is typed IReadOnlyDictionary<string, IIpcRequestHandler>, so the compiler presents a handler that cannot answer a request as if it can.

**Rejected because.** Evidence holds — IIpcServer.cs:30 does derive the streaming interface from IIpcRequestHandler, and DryRunStreamHandler.cs:55-57 throws. But the interface doc at IIpcServer.cs:28-29 states this design decision explicitly ("HandleAsync is never called on a streaming handler … implementations throw from it"), and the present cost is two throwing stubs, one of them in a test. The whole motivation is a hypothetical second consumer of the dispatch dictionary — "a CLI host, a diagnostics endpoint, a new test harness" — none of which exists. That is criterion (c) speculative generality, paid for with a new interface, a type change to the dispatch table in three places, a change to the DI registration, and edits to four test harnesses across 8 files (e). It also collides with the composition-root de-duplication above, which is the change actually worth making to Program.cs:136-160.

#### `profile-store-silently-skips-unreadable-profile-files` — A profile file that fails to deserialize is dropped from the catalog with a log warning, so the profile disappears from the UI and from cross-profile validation

*Lens:* error-handling-failure-modes · *claimed severity:* medium

**Claim.** ProfileStore.LoadAll catches JsonException/IOException per file and continues, returning a Profile list that silently omits the file. The caller cannot distinguish "the user has 3 profiles" from "the user has 4 profiles and one is unreadable", and Save uses the same truncated list as the `otherActive` set for overlap/cycle validation.

**Rejected because.** The evidence is accurate (ProfileStore.cs:49-57 skips per file, :101-109 validates against the truncated list), and the underlying gap is real. Killed on the remedy, which regresses behavior and pre-empts a spec item. (1) The proposal makes ProfileStore.Save return a failure whenever ANY file in the directory is unreadable — one stray or half-written .json in profiles/ would then block the user from saving ANY profile. That is a materially worse failure mode than a profile missing from the list, and it is introduced into the write path of the most safety-relevant store in the app. (2) The in-source comment at :37-39 documents this as a deliberate "Simplification of §2.4's 'load as inactive with a surfaced issue' … Forward-safe — the catalog shape does not change when the richer behavior lands." The proposal changes exactly the catalog shape that note pins, to deliver a different, ad-hoc half of the specified behavior. The correct fix is §2.4 as written (load as inactive, surface the issue), which is a spec-scoped product task, not a 4-file signature refactor. If someone wants a cheap slice today, the acceptable one is raising ProfileStore.cs:51 from LogWarning to LogError and folding the count into EngineHost's startup EngineWarningEvent — no signature change, no new Save failure mode.

#### `servicelauncher-exe-resolution-private` — The FILEMANAGER_SERVICE_EXE override and the side-by-side exe probe are a private static with no test, while their pipe-name counterpart is pinned

*Lens:* testability-seams · *claimed severity:* medium

**Claim.** ServiceLauncher.ResolveServiceExePath implements the documented external override surface (the FILEMANAGER_SERVICE_EXE environment variable) and the fallback probe for "FileManager.Service.exe" beside the UI. It is `private static`, so no test can call it, and grep for "ServiceLauncher" across every tracked file under tests/ returns nothing. Its sibling contract — IpcEndpoint's pipe-name derivation, including the FILEMANAGER_PIPE_NAME override — is pinned by a test that asserts parity between the Contracts and Core.Platform copies.

**Rejected because.** Evidence holds — ResolveServiceExePath is private static at ServiceLauncher.cs:80-86 and nothing under tests/ mentions ServiceLauncher. Killed because the proposed test buys almost nothing for a real cost. The method is six lines with no branching beyond IsNullOrWhiteSpace, and the proposed assertion ("the result is Path.Combine(AppContext.BaseDirectory, \"FileManager.Service.exe\")") literally re-implements the method in the test — a tautology that will never fail for a reason anyone cares about. The price is widening a private member and adding a brand-new InternalsVisibleTo surface to FileManager.Contracts, which currently has no ItemGroup at all, plus process-global environment-variable mutation in a project whose xunit collections run in parallel. The finding names two genuine fragilities (a directory-valued override, a quoted override) and then explicitly declines to fix either — so what it freezes is behavior nobody has argued is correct. Criterion (a)/(e). If this path deserves attention, the change worth proposing is validating/trimming the override at :83-84 and reporting a clearer error, not a characterization test around the current shape.

## Coverage notes

Patterns examined across src/, tests/ and benchmarks/ that came back clean, so their absence from the findings is informative rather than an oversight.

FROZEN FORMATS AND WIRE CONTRACTS — no violations found, and no finding in the roadmap requires one. Every serializable type reachable from Profile, IpcRequest/IpcResponse/EngineEvent, JournalRecord, DispositionAuditRecord, GlobalSettings, PersistedPauseState and UiState is listed in the correct JsonSerializerContext partial; the six contexts are correctly kept separate (internal on-disk shapes are not folded into the public FileManagerJsonContext). The order-as-contract sites are intact: JobPhase's declaration order still matches the progress publisher's backwards-sample drop, and VerificationMethod / RollbackAction / JobOutcome / SkipReason ordinals (int-serialized into the journal) show no reordering. The DryRunReport integer cross-references (SourceIndex/SubjectIndex/DirIndex/ParentIndex/RootDirIndex) are consistently emitted and assembled in one order. The hand-written *.snapshot writer and reader in DryRunSnapshotFormat still agree on all fourteen UTF-8 property literals. Two proposals that would have touched frozen surfaces were explicitly scoped out rather than accepted: the protocol 6→7 bump (deferred to a human decision) and any modification to GlobalSettings (the settings-rebase item works through SettingsService and the ...Serialized shadow properties instead).

AOT AND TRIM DISCIPLINE — clean. No assembly scanning, Activator.CreateInstance, Type.GetType, runtime proxies, config-binding frameworks or attribute-driven discovery of application types anywhere in shipping code. The only production reflection is EnumTitleExtensions.GetTitle reading [Tooltip] off enum field names, and it still carries the [DynamicallyAccessedMembers(PublicFields)] constraint that makes it trim-safe. The one behavior-changing DI proposal in the roadmap (GetServices<IIpcRequestHandler>) was checked against this rule specifically: it enumerates explicit registrations of concrete named types, which is not scanning.

LAYERING — no violations found. References point strictly downward (Contracts ← Core ← Platform.Windows ← hosts); the UI references Contracts only and never Core. The three sanctioned duplications have NOT drifted: EnginePaths.Default() / UiPaths / GlobalSettings.DefaultProfilesDirectory still agree on the same layout, and IpcEndpoint.Resolve() (client) still derives the same pipe name as WindowsIpcEndpointProvider (server). Core contains no OS-specific code beyond the single sanctioned OperatingSystem.IsWindows() probe in NormalizedPath. Two roadmap items were shaped by this constraint rather than fighting it — the save-blocking predicate is hoisted to Contracts (legal) rather than to Core (illegal, since the UI needs it), and IIpcConnection is defined in Contracts because its signatures are BCL-only.

WINDOWS INTEROP — clean. The [GeneratedComInterface] method declaration order for IFileOperation and IShellItem (which is the COM vtable layout, and where a reordering would silently call the wrong shell function and could delete the wrong file) is unmodified, as are the [LibraryImport] entry points and marshalling attributes in WindowsVolumeInfoProvider and WindowsPathCanonicalizer. No finding proposes touching any of it.

ON-DISK INFRASTRUCTURE MARKERS — clean. The .fm_staging / .pipeline_tmp / .fmtmp- names and the StagedPathFor layout are consistent between the writer, the scan exclusions and crash recovery's orphan discovery. The staged-replace consolidation in Tier 2 deliberately preserves the exact path shape; it changes only the guard, not the names.

FROZEN REGIONS — untouched and unassessed by design: third_party/TreeDataGrid (vendored submodule with local modifications), tests/FileManager.Scripts.Windows.Tests/**/profiles/*.json (the de-facto Profile compatibility corpus), the PowerShell environment builders, and BenchmarkDotNet.Artifacts/. Nothing in the roadmap edits any of them.

THE 17 IPC HANDLERS AS A SHAPE — deliberately not reported as duplication. Their similarity is the intentional replacement for reflection-based handler discovery under the AOT constraint. The findings against them are about the registration TABLES being hand-maintained and unguarded, never about the handlers themselves.

DELIBERATE NON-DEAD CODE — verified and left alone: DryRunSnapshotJsonContext (retained as the naive baseline the read-back benchmark measures against), SettingsService.MigrateLegacy and its two legacy string literals (the pre-v2 settings shim), and the [reserved — fails v1 validation] Profile members (SyncMode.Mirror in particular is live in the dry-run path). The four dead-code deletions in Tier 1 were each confirmed by repo-wide grep across .cs, .axaml, .json, .md and .ps1 — including the four x:CompileBindings=\"False\" regions, which bind by the same identifiers.

CONCURRENCY — no defect found. JobOrchestrator's tracked-task/linked-CTS pattern, ScanScheduler's claim/park/re-arm machinery (traced by hand: the two early returns in WorkerLoop exit outside the try's catch, so there is no double-decrement of _liveWorkers today), the DryRunRebuildGate supersede logic and the _applying re-entrancy guard all read correctly. Two items in the roadmap touch this area for OBSERVABILITY only, and one proposal that would have restructured shutdown ordering (IBackgroundWorkTracker) was explicitly rejected as speculative generality against an I-ATOMIC-JOB-governed sequence.

Not assessed at all: runtime performance (nothing was built, run or profiled — the benchmark suite is referenced as a gate, not as evidence), accessibility and visual design of the XAML, the docs/ tree except where cited as normative, and any behavior that only manifests against a real named pipe, a real registry, or a real filesystem under contention.

### Lens notes

- **god-components**: METHOD. Churn was computed over the full history (`git log --format=%h --name-only --since="18 months ago"`), and the repo turns out to be one month old with 128 commits — so a file's commit count is a *share of all development*, not an aging signal. DryRunViewModel.cs at 42/128 (33%) and DryRunEngine.cs at 35/128 (27%) are not merely "hot", they are where essentially all recent work happened. I also computed pairwise co-change over the same window; the top ten pairs are all within the dry-run feature (DryRunViewModel.cs<->DryRunView.axaml 22, <->DryRunViewModelTests.cs 29, DryRunEngine.cs<->DryRunStreamHandler.cs 10, DryRunEngine.cs<->DryRunViewModel.cs 12 — the last being a cross-process, cross-assembly pair). Ranking therefore weighted the dry-run vertical heavily and everything else lightly; all five findings sit in it. That concentration is real, not a lens artifact.

DELIBERATELY NOT REPORTED — large but stable (size alone is never a finding):
- ScanScheduler.cs (566 LOC, 4 nested classes, one `_lock` documented as guarding global thread accounting AND per-volume caps AND every session's parked-work stacks): 3 commits. The single-monitor design is arguably over-coupled, but nobody has needed to change it. Splitting a lock that is currently correct is pure risk with no observed cost.
- JobExecutor.cs (640 LOC, 12 constructor dependencies, 8 phases): 2 commits. CrashRecovery.cs (527 LOC, 6 responsibilities including re-implemented file primitives): 6 commits. AtomicPlacer.cs (402 LOC, 8 deps): 5 commits. These are the durable-safety substrate; they are long because they encode the spec's phase algorithm and I-RECOVER-FIRST ordering step by step, and per rule 7 that line-by-line correspondence to docs/specs/architecture-v1.md is a feature. Low churn confirms they are not where the pain is.
- ProfileValidator.cs (433 LOC, one Validate() fanning out to 10 check groups): 4 commits. This is the normative validation code table cross-referenced by the spec at §; a domain expert must be able to read the codes against the document. Rule 7 applies squarely. Not a finding.
- Job.cs (257 LOC, 20 public types, 10 commits): genuinely a grab-bag, and NormalizedPath — which defines the engine-wide lock order — is buried in a job-model file. I left it out because every one of those 20 types is frozen (JobOutcome/SkipReason ordinals are the on-disk journal's integer wire contract, and JobOutcome member NAMES are stringified into JobSummaryDto and switched on as string literals by ActivityViewModel.cs:98). Moving NormalizedPath to its own file is legal, but it is file organization with no measured cost, and the do-not-break register makes the surrounding types un-splittable. Not worth the risk budget.
- PathTruncation.cs / the Controls folder (602 LOC combined): 3 commits, and the pure rules are already extracted UI-free with tests. Correctly factored.

DELIBERATELY NOT REPORTED — organization rather than responsibility:
- "DryRunViewModel.cs is 2751 lines / 20 top-level types, split the file." Raising this standalone would be a file-layout finding, which rule 6 excludes. The author already marked the six boundaries with banner comments (lines 22, 318, 1000, 1153, 2105, 2227), so the split is known and uncontested. I folded it into finding #1's proposedChange as a same-namespace file move, where it rides along with a change that has an actual cost attached.
- DryRunView.axaml (681 lines, 28 commits, 26% of all XAML). I checked whether the two tab markup blocks duplicate each other the way the view models do: after normalizing `Sources.`/`Destinations.` and the row type, the two ~140-line blocks differ by 86 lines — about half, not the ~85% the C# shows. That is real but much weaker, and the fix (a shared tab DataTemplate or UserControl) is best done as a follow-on once finding #1 lands and the two tabs share a base type. Not raised separately.
- SettingsViewModel.cs (575 LOC, 11 commits, 6 nominal responsibilities). I read it looking for the seam and did not find a compelling one. BuildCatalog is a declarative data block; ApplyFilter/BuildNavigation are small; the undo integration is delegated to UndoHistory; ChangeProfilesDirectory is one command with a callback seam and a try/finally. The parts are already separable by reading, and the tests are already split (SettingsViewModelTests, SettingsViewModelUndoTests, SettingsSearchTests). Per the brief's instruction: this one is closer to genuinely cohesive-despite-size than to a god class, and I am saying so rather than inventing a split.
- The 17 IIpcRequestHandler implementations. Explicitly excluded by the brief as the intentional AOT-safe replacement for reflection-based discovery. My finding #3 targets DryRunStreamHandler for carrying pipeline orchestration, which is a different complaint from their shape similarity, and it is careful not to disturb the RequestType key or the Program.cs dispatch list.

DELIBERATELY NOT REPORTED — other lenses' territory:
- The batched dry-run path (DryRunRequest / DryRunHandler / IDryRunEngine.SimulateAsync / ReportBuilder / the byte-budget machinery) has no UI client: `grep -rn 'DryRunStreamRequest\|DryRunRequest' src/FileManager.UI/` returns exactly one line and it is the *stream* request. That is a dead-code / wire-surface question, not an SRP one, so I noted it inside finding #4's proposedChange as a decision to make rather than raising it as its own finding. Note DryRunRequest is on the frozen [JsonDerivedType] discriminator table, so deleting it would require a protocol version bump — do not treat it as free.
- Test-suite duplication (three copies of FakeSettings, four IVolumeInfoProvider doubles, three PolicySnapshot factories with disagreeing defaults, JobExecutorTests hand-composing the 12-collaborator graph the shared harness already builds). All real, all in-scope paths, but they are duplication findings, and the harness/fixture churn is low. Left for that lens.
- EnginePaths vs UiPaths vs GlobalSettings.DefaultProfilesDirectory. The brief marks this as sanctioned duplication under §1 rule 3; I checked the three copies still agree and did not raise it.

BLAST-RADIUS DISCIPLINE. Every call-site number above came from a grep I ran, and I named the grep in the notes field so it can be re-run. Two proposals were deliberately narrowed after checking the do-not-break register: finding #2 leaves all 11 DryRunTreeNode [RelayCommand] methods in place because DryRunView.axaml binds them inside four `x:CompileBindings="False"` regions where a rename is a silent dead menu item rather than a build error; finding #3 constructs the extracted pipeline inline instead of registering it, so Program.cs's hand-maintained DI list and dispatch table stay untouched.

**duplication**: WHAT I LOOKED FOR: copy-pasted blocks with renamed identifiers (diffed candidate regions mechanically after normalizing type names rather than eyeballing them); the same non-obvious rule restated (formulas, magic thresholds, exception filters, resource-key vocabularies); sibling modules implementing the same lifecycle; hand-maintained parallel tables in one file; near-identical overloads.

METHOD NOTE: the two strongest findings were confirmed by mechanical diff, not by shape. DryRunSourcesTab vs DryRunDestinationsTab: 391 of 451/500 lines identical after renaming only the row type, including one 96-line byte-identical run (verified with `diff` on extracted ranges). That is the difference between "these look alike" and "these are the same code".

DELIBERATELY NOT REPORTED:

1. The 17 IIpcRequestHandler implementations as a duplication candidate. They are the explicit, AOT-mandated replacement for reflection-based dispatch (§4.9); their shape similarity is the design. I reported only the Program.cs list-written-twice, which is copy-paste of names with no compile-time link — a different problem.

2. EnginePaths ↔ UiPaths ↔ GlobalSettings.DefaultProfilesDirectory/DefaultScratchDirectory. Sanctioned triplication (§1 rule 3: the UI may reference Contracts only). I checked all three for drift and they agree today (%LOCALAPPDATA%\FileManager\{profiles,scratch,logs,settings.json}); consolidating would break the layering rule.

3. SystemDrives.Classify (UI, over DriveType) vs WindowsVolumeInfoProvider.GetDriveClass (Platform.Windows, over GetDriveTypeW). Same cross-assembly rule, but the UI cannot reference Core/Platform. I verified the two mappings agree member-for-member. Both carry comments pointing at each other. Leave it.

4. IpcEndpoint.Resolve() vs WindowsIpcEndpointProvider pipe-name derivation. Deliberately duplicated per §4.11; a Platform.Windows test already asserts parity.

5. GlobalSettings' paired [JsonIgnore] getter + [JsonInclude] "…Serialized" shadow property, written twice (ScratchDirectory :40-70, ProfilesDirectory :78-105). It is genuinely one non-obvious rule (absent-vs-default collapsing) restated — but the type is frozen, the properties cannot move, and a shared helper would save about two lines per copy. Not worth touching a persisted-format type for.

6. SourceRowViewModel vs TargetRowViewModel (Editor/EditorRows.cs:10-52). ~10 duplicated lines differing by a picker-title string; the one real shared rule (StartNear) is already extracted into RowBrowsing. Merging them would collapse two x:DataType-visible types for negligible gain.

7. DriveTypeOverrideRowViewModel / SpecificDriveOverrideRowViewModel / AutoNumberSettingViewModel repeating the Auto/Value/ShowValue/OnAutoChanged/UndoableProperties block. Five lines of MVVM boilerplate over source-generated observable properties, and the three are DataTemplate type keys. Excluded by the lens's own "boilerplate property declarations" rule.

8. ActivityRow's three parallel switches (StatusText/StatusIconKey/StatusColorKey, ActivityViewModel.cs:85-111) over the same JobOutcome string vocabulary. Same shape as the DestinationRowKind finding but only three sites over five cases, all within thirty lines of each other, and its keys ARE covered by ResourceKeyContractTests. Below the bar; the dry-run one is seven sites spread over 1900 lines with no guard test.

9. Three debounce/supersede mechanisms (ProfileListViewModel's hand-rolled CTS+Task.Delay at :153-193, DryRunRebuildGate, SettingsViewModel's synchronous filtering). They answer different requirements — a small in-memory name filter, a 500k-row off-thread rebuild, and an explicitly-documented decision to filter synchronously — and SettingsViewModel.cs:205-208 already documents why it diverges. Merging them would produce one gate with three masters.

10. CrashRecovery.CopyFlush vs AtomicPlacer.CopyToTempAsync, and CrashRecovery.SafeDelete vs the placer's delete handling. Structurally similar but one is synchronous with throw-on-failure semantics (recovery runs before the host starts, sync by design) and the other is async returning Result<,JobError>. Different error contracts, different reasons to change. Only the File.Replace fallback — where the copies have measurably drifted — met the bar.

11. RollbackExecutor.TryReplace's File.Replace fallback. Same three-exception filter as the other two, but it replaces in the opposite direction with a different fallback (overwrite:true). Explicitly excluded from the StagedReplace extraction for that reason.

12. All test-side duplication flagged in the structural map (three FakeSettings copies, four IVolumeInfoProvider doubles, three PolicySnapshot factories, JobExecutorTests hand-composing the graph the harness builds). Per the lens rules, test duplication is load-bearing unless it hides a bug, and I found no evidence it does here. The one item worth a separate lens is JobExecutorHarness.cs:198, whose comment documents a suspected production cancellation/cleanup race in the placer — that is a correctness lead, not duplication.

13. DryRunItemActions.OpenFile and OpenFolderInExplorer both delegating to ShellOpen (DryRunItemActions.cs:148, :150). Real identical-body duplication, but two lines, and the interface documents them as different operations that DryRunTreeNode selects between by IsDirectory. Collapsing them would erase a deliberate seam.

14. DryRunEngine's four UpperBoundBytes overloads (:850-862). Overloads over different types with different fields, correctly delegating to a shared StringUpperBound. Not duplication.

FOUND WHILE LOOKING, NOT A DUPLICATION FINDING: tests/FileManager.UI.Tests/ResourceKeyContractTests.cs enumerates only ActivityRow's keys. "IconUntouched", "IconAdd", "IconTrash" and "Brush.Warning" are emitted by DryRunViewModel/DryRunDestinationsTab and resolved at runtime, but no test asserts they exist in App.axaml. I folded fixing that into the destination-row-kind finding since a single table makes it a one-line test change.

**dead-code**: Method: for every candidate I ran a repo-wide `grep -rn` for the bare identifier across ALL file types (.cs, .axaml, .md, .json, .ps1, .csproj, .slnx), excluding only third_party/ and bin/obj, and cross-checked the DO-NOT-BREAK register before reporting. I also ran two scripted passes over src/: (a) identifiers whose total repo occurrence count equals their declaration count, and (b) identifiers with zero references outside their declaring file in src/. Findings 1-3 and 7 are PROVEN dead (zero references by any mechanism). Findings 4-6 are test-only-reachable and I state exactly what stays.

DELIBERATELY NOT REPORTED:

1. The dormant spec seams — src/FileManager.Core/Transformers/ (ITransformerChainRunner, IProcessRunner, ITokenExpander, IArgumentParser), src/FileManager.Core/Watching/IWatcherService.cs / ISettleTracker.cs / ISchedulerService.cs / IReadinessProbe.cs, and src/FileManager.Core/Platform/IShellIntegration.cs. These have zero implementations and zero call sites in src/ — the largest single block of unreferenced code in scope. I am not proposing deletion: each is declared verbatim in the normative spec (docs/specs/architecture-v1.md §4.2/§4.5/§4.11, e.g. lines 388, 408, 423, 447, 746, 767, 796, 814, 1326) and tracked as planned-not-built in docs/specs/implementation-progress.md:82-83,103,149-150. They are interface declarations only (~60 LOC each, no bodies), so the cost paid today is near zero, and rule 7 (code mirroring an external spec line-by-line) plus the register's treatment of the spec as frozen both apply. Do not re-raise this without a decision to cut those features from the roadmap.

2. The batched dry-run path (DryRunEngine.SimulateAsync, ReportBuilder, MaxReportBytes, DryRunHandler, DryRunRequest, DryRunResponse). Confirmed: src/FileManager.UI references only DryRunStreamRequest, so nothing in the shipping UI calls the batched path. But DryRunRequest/DryRunResponse are frozen wire types with [JsonDerivedType] discriminators, ProtocolVersion 6 depends on them, and dry-run-pooling-plan.md:36 records the batched path as the CLI's entry point. Deleting the handler would turn `dry-run` into NOT_IMPLEMENTED at runtime with no compile error. The register forbids this without a migration story and I cannot supply one.

3. DryRunSnapshotJsonContext — flagged as unused by production, but the register and its own doc say it is retained on purpose as the naïve baseline that DryRunSpoolReadbackBenchmarks.cs:52,69 measures the trimmed hand-written format against. Not dead.

4. SettingsService.MigrateLegacy and the "DryRunConcurrencyMode"/"DryRunManualWorkers" string literals — look like dead pre-v2 code; they are a back-compat shim for settings.json written by older builds. Register explicitly protects them.

5. BoolSettingViewModel + Setting.Bool (src/FileManager.UI/ViewModels/Settings/SettingItems.cs:208,260) — never constructed by BuildCatalog or any test, but SettingsWindow.axaml:85 declares a type-keyed DataTemplate for it and the class comment says the absence from the catalog is deliberate. Deleting it means deleting the template too; ~25 LOC, and the register treats setting-editor VM type names as a runtime-resolved public API. Low value, real risk.

6. EngineConfig.ExecutableAllowlist and EngineConfig.LaunchTrayOnStart (src/FileManager.Core/EngineConfig.cs:10-11) — provably unread in src/ and tests/. Not reported: the record is reproduced verbatim in docs/specs/architecture-v1.md:2362, and implementation-progress.md:195 records EngineConfig as "registered with defaults only", i.e. known-incomplete rather than dead. Two initializers, zero runtime cost.

7. EngineEventPump.Faulted (src/FileManager.UI/Services/EngineEventPump.cs:41) — assigned only by tests/FileManager.UI.Tests/EngineEventPumpTests.cs:72; App.axaml.cs:80-84 wires Event and Connected but not Faulted, so a stream fault reaches no view model. It is a one-property seam with a live invocation site (line 65). Deleting it is churn and would erase the marker for a gap somebody may want to close; it belongs to a "hidden failure path" review, not a deletion review.

8. ViewModelBase (src/FileManager.UI/ViewModels/ViewModelBase.cs:5) — an empty abstract class over ObservableObject carrying no members or invariant, but it is the declared base of 20 view models. Removing it edits 20 files to delete nothing; that is not a deletion win.

9. Test-seam members that look unused: UndoHistory.UndoDepth/RedoDepth, EvaluationCarrierPool.RetainedCount/RentedEvaluations/ReturnedEvaluations, DryRunEngine.SpoolFactory, ProfileListViewModel.SearchDebounce. Each is documented in-source as a test seam and each has test call sites. Not dead.

10. False positives my scripts raised and I discarded after reading: IFilter.Excludes (6 implementations reached through the interface at IFilterCompiler.cs:48), CompositeChange (used at UndoHistory.cs:164), MeasureOverride on PathText/StorageBar (Avalonia framework overrides), Program.Main x2, and all [RelayCommand] methods (DismissNotice, OpenSettings, ExportProfiles, ImportProfiles, AddTarget, RemoveTarget/RemoveSource) whose generated *Command properties are bound in .axaml.

11. No commented-out code blocks exist in src/ — grep for commented `if/for/while/return/var/public/private/await/foreach` lines found only prose comments that wrap onto a continuation line. The only conditional compilation is a single `#if DEBUG` at src/FileManager.UI/Program.cs:56. DryRunStreamHandler.HandleAsync's `throw new NotSupportedException` is unreachable by construction but is required by the IIpcStreamingRequestHandler : IIpcRequestHandler inheritance and is documented as such; removing it needs an interface-hierarchy change, not a deletion.

**layering**: Scope: all of src/, tests/, benchmarks/ (349 files). Verified project-reference direction first — it is clean and matches the spec's hard rule: Contracts (no PackageReference at all) ← Core ← Platform.Windows ← Service; UI references Contracts + TreeDataGrid only, with the Service reference marked ReferenceOutputAssembly="false" (FileManager.UI.csproj:32). No project cycle, no upward project reference, no assembly scanning / Activator.CreateInstance / Type.GetType anywhere.

DELIBERATELY NOT REPORTED:

1. DryRunViewModel.cs importing Avalonia (the only file under ViewModels/ that does — lines 1-3, HierarchicalTreeDataGridSource at 338/1199/1654, HierarchicalRow walk at 524-531). This looked like the headline finding for an Avalonia lens, but the cost is not being paid: DryRunViewModelTests.cs constructs the VM with no Application and no HeadlessCollection, and asserts against TreeSource (lines 831, 1100, 1154) and ExpandAllCommand (851) successfully. HierarchicalTreeDataGridSource IS TreeDataGrid's MVVM binding surface — the alternative is an abstraction layer over a control API, which rule 8 forbids. The rest of the file is scrupulously framework-free (TreePill carries resource-key strings precisely so it stays Avalonia-free, line 322-326).

2. Code-behind in MainWindow.axaml.cs (201 LOC), DryRunView.axaml.cs (190 LOC), SettingsWindow.axaml.cs (141 LOC). I read all three looking for business logic. It is all genuine view-interaction work that cannot live in a view model: GridSplitter double-tap detection via ClickCount because the splitter marks pointer input handled (MainWindow.axaml.cs:31-38), WindowState glyph sync, the async-void two-pass OnClosing handshake, KeyGesture matching, and TreeDataGridCell focus restoration after the flattened row list rebuilds (DryRunView.axaml.cs:142-153). Every decision that is policy rather than input is already delegated to the VM (RequestCloseAsync, SaveSidebarState, MinExpandedSidebarWidth). Reporting these would be pure churn.

3. Direct File/JsonSerializer IO in MainWindowViewModel.ImportProfiles (lines 527-528) with no ProfileImport seam, while the export path routes through Services/ProfileExport. Asymmetric, and it is real IO in a view model — but tests/FileManager.UI.Tests/ProfileImportExportTests.cs already covers both directions end-to-end against a temp directory (8 command executions), so the "cannot be tested" cost is not being paid. Adding an IProfileFileStore seam would buy only the removal of temp-dir setup from one test class.

4. DryRunFileRow/DryRunDestinationRow/DryRunTreeNode calling System.IO.File.Exists in CanExecute (DryRunViewModel.cs:75, 274, 516-518). A VM touching the filesystem, but it is a right-click-time existence probe on a path the user is looking at — routing it through an injected seam would add an interface for one predicate and make the menu's greying-out harder to reason about.

5. The three sanctioned-duplication tables named in the do-not-break register. I diffed all three rather than assuming: UiPaths (%LOCALAPPDATA%\FileManager, logs, settings.json) matches EnginePaths.Default() exactly; GlobalSettings.DefaultProfilesDirectory matches EnginePaths.ProfilesDirectory; SystemDrives.Classify (SystemDrives.cs:78-86) maps the same five DriveType values to the same five DriveClass values as WindowsVolumeInfoProvider.GetDriveClass (lines 116-124). No drift. Consolidating any of them would violate §1 rule 3 (UI references Contracts only). Note that finding #1 is NOT this — it is about a static default winning over an injected value inside Core, which is a different defect.

6. The 17 IPC handlers' shape similarity, and IpcEndpoint being duplicated between Contracts and Core.Platform — both explicitly sanctioned by the register as the AOT-mandated replacement for reflective discovery (§4.9, §4.11). Finding #5 targets only the redundant SECOND list in Program.cs, not the handlers.

7. IIpcStreamingRequestHandler deriving from IIpcRequestHandler, which forces DryRunStreamHandler.HandleAsync to `throw new NotSupportedException` (DryRunStreamHandler.cs:55-57) — a genuine LSP violation, unreachable by construction because IpcServer.cs:184 type-tests for the streaming interface first. One throw statement; the fix (splitting the interfaces and widening the dispatch dictionary's value type) costs more churn than the defect.

8. ServiceLauncher living in Contracts and calling Process.Start with a hardcoded "FileManager.Service.exe" (ServiceLauncher.cs:16, 38) — arguably OS/process concerns in the BCL-only DTO layer, but the register freezes both the exe name and the env-var override as an external operational contract, and the UI (which can reference nothing else) is the only caller.

9. StartupTheme reading the service's settings.json directly off disk from the UI process (App.axaml.cs:31, UiPaths.cs:20) — a cross-process read of another component's file. Documented in-source as a deliberate first-paint optimisation, reconciled over IPC in window.Opened (App.axaml.cs:94-96), and listed in the register as a known two-reader/one-writer format.

10. The six modal-dialog Func/Action seams assigned inline in App.axaml.cs:42-72, each defaulting to null meaning "proceed" so headless tests silently take the unconfirmed path on delete/run/import. This is a real hazard but it is a test-fidelity/default-safety issue rather than a layering one, and the destructive paths (run, delete) are additionally guarded service-side by ProfileValidator's blocking warnings.

11. Global mutable state: I searched for it specifically and found none. No mutable statics in src/ outside `static readonly` and consts; Core/Contracts/Platform.Windows never touch Serilog's static Log (all ILogger-injected); only two Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable reads exist, both documented override surfaces.

**divergent-modules**: WHAT I COMPARED. Three sibling sets, across construct/configure/validate/execute/present/persist plus interface conformance, naming, error handling and wiring:
(1) src/FileManager.Core/IPC/Handlers/ — all 17 IIpcRequestHandler implementations read end to end, plus the Service-side ShutdownHandler, IpcServer's dispatch/invoke path, and the Program.cs registration table.
(2) src/FileManager.UI/ViewModels/Settings/ — SettingItems (4 editor kinds + factories), SettingsRows (2 override rows), DriveOverridesSettingViewModel, SettingsCategoryViewModel/SettingsNavNodeViewModel, and their consumer SettingsViewModel + the SettingsWindow.axaml DataTemplate keys.
(3) src/FileManager.Platform.Windows/ — all six Windows*Provider/Service/Registrar/Preserver/Canonicalizer adapters against their Core/Platform ports.
Plus two adjacent parallel sets the map pointed at: the dry-run row types in DryRunViewModel.cs, and the batched-vs-streamed dry-run pipelines.

DELIBERATELY NOT REPORTED, with reasons:

- The 17 handlers' shape similarity. Explicitly the point (AOT: no reflection-based discovery, §4.9). Their per-handler ILogger/collaborator lists differ because their collaborators differ. Not divergence.
- Ad-hoc error-code strings per handler (PROFILE_DELETE_FAILED, RECENT_JOBS_FAILED, SET_PAUSED_FAILED, JOB_LOG_UNREADABLE, …) with no shared constant table. I checked what the UI actually matches: only "JOB_LOG_NOT_FOUND" (ActivityViewModel.cs:312) and "IPC_TRANSPORT"/"IPC_UNEXPECTED_RESPONSE"/"IPC_MALFORMED" (IpcGateway.cs:248) and "IPC_TRANSPORT" (DryRunViewModel.cs:2403). Every other code is only displayed. Introducing a constants table would be pure principle with no cost being paid today, and the codes are pinned as a string-reference contract in the do-not-break register.
- Delete-of-a-nonexistent-profile answering OkResponse while GetProfile answers PROFILE_NOT_FOUND for the same id. ProfileStore.Delete is documented as idempotent (File.Delete on a missing file is a no-op, ProfileStore.cs:178). Idempotent delete is a legitimate, deliberate semantic, not drift.
- Handlers that ignore the CancellationToken. I traced which collaborators can produce Result.Canceled: within Core only DryRunEngine.SimulateAsync, AtomicPlacer, FileHasher and JobExecutor do, and the only one on a handler path is SimulateAsync — which DryRunHandler does check (DryRunHandler.cs:32). No sibling is silently dropping a cancelled result.
- RelocateProfilesHandler carrying its own catch-all when IpcServer.InvokeAsync already converts a handler throw to INTERNAL_ERROR (IpcServer.cs:272-276). The local catch produces a domain code and a user-readable message instead of a raw exception message; that is a better answer, not a divergent one.
- The Auto/Value/ShowValue/OnAutoChanged/UndoableProperties block repeated three times (SettingItems.cs:187-203, SettingsRows.cs:17-30, SettingsRows.cs:50-65). Real duplication, but C# single inheritance means at most two of the three could share a base (AutoNumberSettingViewModel must derive from SettingItemViewModel; the two rows derive from ViewModelBase), the shared surface is ~10 lines, and the one behavioural difference — Minimum is a bound property on the setting and a hardcoded Minimum="1" in the row DataTemplates (SettingsWindow.axaml:76 vs 122/160) — is neutralised at save time by ToBudget's Math.Max(1, value) (SettingsViewModel.cs:574). No cost is being paid.
- SourceRowViewModel vs TargetRowViewModel (EditorRows.cs:10 and 34). Near-identical, but the shared rule is already extracted into RowBrowsing.StartNear (line 59), what remains is ~8 lines plus a picker title string, and Source carries two settle/stability properties Target genuinely does not have.
- The six Windows adapters. I looked hard for divergence here and found consistency instead: every one is [SupportedOSPlatform("windows")], every one takes ILogger via primary constructor, every one has a documented last-resort catch that degrades to a Result failure or a documented best-effort fallback. WindowsIpcEndpointProvider returning Result.Canceled() on OperationCanceledException while others do not is correct — it is the only one with a cancellable await. The Sweep/IsNetworkPath/GetDriveClass layering inside WindowsVolumeInfoProvider is one adapter's internal structure, not cross-sibling drift.
- SystemDrives.Classify (src/FileManager.UI/Services/SystemDrives.cs:77) re-deriving the DriveType→DriveClass mapping that WindowsVolumeInfoProvider.GetDriveClass owns. This is sanctioned duplication under the §1 rule that the UI references Contracts only; consolidating it would break layering. I verified the two mappings agree member for member today, so there is nothing to flag.
- EnginePaths / UiPaths / GlobalSettings.DefaultProfilesDirectory triple. Same reason — the register names it sanctioned. I checked the three for drift and they agree.
- IUndoTrackable (Undo/UndoableProperty.cs:43). This is the counter-example worth recording: it is exactly the shared contract the settings siblings needed, it already exists, it is delegate-based rather than reflective (AOT-correct), and it has a TrackNested default-interface hook for the non-scalar case. Nothing to fix.
- IpcGateway's 14 methods. All but three funnel through one generic RequestAsync<TResponse,TValue>; the three exceptions (SubscribeEventsAsync, DryRunAsync, SaveProfileAsync) each carry a documented reason for their own connection or post-processing. Uniform by construction.

**failure-modes**: WHAT I LOOKED FOR: all 313 catch sites under src/, plus every place a Result<T,E> error is discarded, every method returning an empty collection/default on a fault, and disposal on failure paths.

This codebase has already been through a no-silent-failure pass — most catch blocks carry an explicit "Last-resort catch-and-log (directive)" comment at a genuine task/loop boundary and re-shape the fault into a Result. I deliberately did NOT report those. The defects that survive are all the same shape: a fault IS captured into a value or a log line, but the value never reaches the process boundary where the user is. That is why four of the six findings converge on EngineWarningEvent — a fully implemented wire type (Contracts/IPC/EngineEvent.cs:86) that MainWindowViewModel already routes to the activity notice bar (line 342) and that no production code in src/ ever publishes.

DELIBERATELY NOT REPORTED:
- Every catch at an application entry point or fire-and-forget loop: EngineHost.ExecuteAsync:51, JobOrchestrator.ConsumeAsync:112 and RunJobAsync:184, EngineEventPump.RunAsync:87, IpcServer's accept/serve loops, UI Program.cs:41, MainWindow.axaml.cs:191. Correct design per the brief. JobOrchestrator's consumer catch is exemplary — it sets _pipelineFaulted AND _lastError with a comment explaining that logging alone was not enough.
- EngineEventPump.Faulted (line 41) is assigned only in tests; App.axaml.cs:80-84 wires Event and Connected but not Faulted. Genuinely "error state never read", but the cost is nil: the pump reconnects with backoff and its Connected hook calls ReconcileEngineStateAsync, which re-seeds authoritative state, and StatusBarViewModel's independent poll loop owns the connection caption. Reporting it would be principle-only.
- ScanScheduler.WorkerLoop's outer catch (line 126) decrements _liveWorkers and retires the thread; if it fired while work was claimed, the session's channel would never complete and Consume() would block forever. I traced every path and could not reach it — Process() catches Exception around its whole body and always calls session.Complete, and TryClaimLocked cannot throw given how _pending/_volumeOrder/_volumes are maintained. Unreachable-by-construction, so not a finding, but it is the one place in the repo where a swallowed exception would deadlock rather than degrade.
- ConflictResolver's reliance on File.Exists (lines 42/49/107): File.Exists returns false on access-denied, so an unreadable destination is treated as absent and routed to Write. The subsequent placer write fails loudly with a JobError, so the failure is not hidden — only misattributed.
- SettingsService.Update using a fixed "<final>.tmp" temp name (line 51) while ProfileStore deliberately randomizes for exactly this reason (comment at ProfileStore.cs:120). Two concurrent settings writes collide on FileShare.None, but that surfaces as a returned error, not a silent one. Out of lens.
- Best-effort cleanup catches that log and continue where the operation is genuinely cosmetic: ProfileStore.TryDeleteTemp, RelocateProfilesHandler.RollBackCopies and its Phase-3 delete loop, JobExecutor.CleanUpPlacementArtifacts, EngineHost.PurgeScratchDirectory, PathText.cs:122. Each is preceded by a durable commit; a failure leaves reclaimable disk, not wrong data.
- CrashRecovery's per-job catch (line 86) logs and leaves the job for the next startup — and the journal rotation that follows preserves un-closed jobs, so this is correct. It only decrements the "recovered" counter, which is log-only anyway. The adjacent sync-over-async at line 457 is a different lens.
- UI view-model command catches (MainWindowViewModel, ProfileEditorViewModel, ExportProfilesViewModel, DryRunViewModel): every one sets a user-visible ErrorMessage/LocalError banner. ExportProfilesViewModel:126 even collects per-item failures rather than aborting the batch. Nothing hidden.
- DiskPreflight is the model the rest of the engine should follow — it explicitly fails closed on an unresolvable volume with a comment saying why (line 27). Cited here so a future review does not "simplify" it.

**testability**: COVERAGE MAP (the governing output). 110 test files / ~893 [Fact]+[Theory] cases against 213 source files, 5 test projects.

WELL COVERED — safe to refactor behind existing tests:
- Journal + crash recovery: CrashRecoveryTests (1085 LOC), JobJournalTests, NdjsonFrameTests, RollbackExecutorTests. The highest-data-loss subsystem is also the best tested.
- Job execution: four harness-based suites (JobExecutorFileOperation 1459 LOC, Disposition, FailureRollback, Concurrency) plus Orchestrator/PlanFactory/ProgressPublisher/StateMachine.
- Placement: AtomicPlacer, ConflictResolverProbe, FileHasher, SourcePriorityRegistry, TransientRetryPolicy.
- Dry run engine + streaming: DryRunEngineTests (965), DryRunPipelineTests (410), DestinationProjector, SpaceEstimator, FileDryRunSpool, and DryRunStreamHandlerTests (405, 9 facts incl. mirror sweep, sweep cap, throttled progress).
- Wire contracts: SerializationTests (599) round-trips every discriminator; IpcRequestTypesTests pins two of three dispatch legs; IpcFrameCodecTests; DryRunDirectoryTableTests.
- IpcClient's streaming reassembly, poison recovery and mid-stream faults: IpcServerStreamingTests + IpcRobustnessTests over real named pipes.
- UI view models: DryRunViewModel (1591 LOC of tests + memory probes + smoke), MainWindowViewModel (4 suites incl. the full import/export path with real temp files), ProfileEditor, ProfileList, Settings (+undo), Activity, StatusBar, UndoHistory, PathTruncation, StartupTheme, UiStateStore, ResourceKeyContractTests.

NO COVERAGE, WRITE CHARACTERIZATION TESTS BEFORE ANY STRUCTURAL CHANGE (ranked):
1. src/FileManager.Service/EngineHost.cs — the entire startup ordering. Blocks any FileManager.Service refactor. (finding 1)
2. src/FileManager.Service/Program.cs — DI graph + dispatch table; the E2E test's copy has already drifted to 14 of 17 handlers. (finding 2)
3. src/FileManager.UI/Services/IpcGateway.cs — 328 LOC, no test file at all. (finding 3)
4. src/FileManager.Core/Scanning/ScanScheduler.cs worker pool — 692 LOC, 5 tests, none observing the thread pool. (finding 4)
5. src/FileManager.Core/Scheduling/CronExpression.cs — zero references from tests/. (finding 5)
6. src/FileManager.UI/Controls/StorageBar.cs band logic. (finding 6)
7. src/FileManager.Contracts/IPC/ServiceLauncher.cs. (finding 7)
8. src/FileManager.Service/ShutdownHandler.cs — the 17th handler, internal, zero tests, hardcoded 250ms Task.Delay with no TimeProvider. Folded into finding 1's InternalsVisibleTo edit rather than raised separately: once the IVT lands it is directly constructible, and its only untestable element (the real-time delay) is documented as best-effort with a caller that tolerates a lost ack.
9. src/FileManager.Platform.Windows/WindowsPathCanonicalizer.cs — the only one of the six Windows adapters with no test file, and it feeds ProfileValidator's containment checks. NOT raised as a finding: exercising the 8.3-expansion branch requires 8dot3name enabled on the test volume, which is machine-dependent and would produce a flaky test. Worth a manual note, not an automated one.

DELIBERATELY NOT REPORTED:
- DryRunSnapshotFormat.cs (231 LOC, hand-written/hand-read persisted format, no test file bearing its name). I initially flagged it, then verified DryRunEngineTests.Spilled_stream_report_is_content_identical_to_the_unpooled_in_memory_run (line 706) forces a spill over a mix of New/SkipUnchanged/Overwrite and diffs the assembled result against the in-memory baseline — which does cover the two dangerous omitted-field reconstructions (source op path/root, and dest op path when SubjectIndex >= 0). It is covered end-to-end, just not by name. The one real gap is the corrupt-SubjectIndex IOException guard at DryRunSnapshotFormat.cs:178; too narrow to justify a finding.
- IpcClient.DryRunStreamAsync's IPC_MALFORMED guards (bad ParentIndex / out-of-range directory index, lines 251-268). Uncovered, but the existing ChunkedDryRunHandler in IpcServerStreamingTests can emit a bad table with a two-line change — that is a test to add, not a seam to build, and it does not gate any refactor.
- The 17 IPC handlers' shape similarity, and the fact that 8 of them have no dedicated handler test. Per the do-not-break register the parallel-handler set is the intentional AOT replacement for reflection discovery; the 8 untested ones are thin request-cast + single-collaborator-call + Result-map, all exercised over the pipe by EndToEndSmokeTests. Consolidating or generifying them is explicitly out of bounds, and finding 2 gives the dispatch table the guard that actually matters.
- Views code-behind: MainWindow's two-pass close handshake (_closing/_closeConfirmed re-entrancy guard, MainWindow.axaml.cs:153-199), DryRunView's six keyboard gestures, SettingsWindow's scroll-to-setting anchor lookup. All uncovered, and the close guard fixes a real documented bug (a second close attempt firing a second service shutdown). Not raised because the guard lives in an `async void` override that the framework does not await — any test would be racing the teardown, and a flaky test on a shutdown path is worse than none. The VM half (MainWindowViewModel.RequestCloseAsync) IS covered by MainWindowViewModelCloseTests.
- Test-suite hygiene the mapping phase surfaced (nine fakes in one Fakes.cs, three duplicate FakeSettings, four IVolumeInfoProvider doubles, three divergent PolicySnapshot factories, JobExecutorTests hand-composing the graph the harness already builds, the two empty UnitTest1 templates, fixed Task.Delay used as synchronization). Real duplication, but it is duplication *inside the tests* — it does not make any production code untestable, and churning the test project is exactly the churn this review is meant to avoid. The one exception worth flagging to whoever fixes finding 2: DryRunEngineTests.cs:83 constructs SourceScanner without the optional IVolumeInfoProvider that production always passes, so the largest dry-run suite runs a scanner configuration the product never ships.
- Contracts holding non-DTO material (ByteSize.Format, TooltipAttribute, DryRunDirectoryTableBuilder). All three are already tested; a move would break the §1 layering rule that the UI references Contracts only.
- EnginePaths / UiPaths / GlobalSettings.DefaultProfilesDirectory triplication. Sanctioned by §1 rule 3 and explicitly called out in the register as not-to-consolidate. No test pins the three copies against each other, but a test cannot: UI.Tests cannot see Core. Left alone.
- Everything under third_party/TreeDataGrid/ and tests/FileManager.Scripts.Windows.Tests/ (frozen regions).

### Run health

- All 7 lenses ran; none were skipped.
- 41 candidates → 41 verified → 30 kept, 11 killed. No finding was dropped unverified.
- Severity spread is 5 high / 11 medium / 14 low, so the run is not uniformly low-severity noise.
- Every file path cited as *evidence* (106 distinct paths) was checked against the working tree and resolves. Paths appearing only in *proposed change* / *verification* text are new files the roadmap asks you to create, and do not exist yet by design.
- `tests/FileManager.Scripts.Windows.Tests/` is real but contains no `.cs` files (PowerShell environment-builder scripts plus fixture `profiles/*.json`), so it is absent from the 50,762 LOC inventory while still holding frozen-format fixture data. Treat its fixtures as covered by the Profile freeze.
- `FileManager.Cli`, specified in `docs/specs/architecture-v1.md` §2.1, does not exist yet. That is unbuilt scope, not drift, and no finding treats it as a defect.
- The review reads the tree at commit `12a31d5`. The `third_party/TreeDataGrid` submodule was dirty at run time and was excluded from review by design.
